Module 4

Machine code and assembly language

A processor does not run C, batch files or shell scripts. It runs bytes: it fetches a few bytes from memory, decodes them as one instruction, executes that instruction and moves on to the next. Earlier modules met such code many times, in the boot sectors of Module 1 and the INT 21h dispatcher of Module 2, but always through the source. This module reads the bytes themselves. It covers the two instruction sets of the course: the 16-bit real-mode code of the 8086, in which MS-DOS 4.00 and its programs are written, and the 64-bit x86-64 (amd64) code that FreeBSD 15.1 runs. A current PC processor still executes both; after a BIOS boot it starts in real mode (Module 1, section 1.1). The tools are the ones each system offers: MS-DOS 4.00's own DEBUG and the MASM 5.10 assembler that built MS-DOS, NASM for both systems, and on FreeBSD clang's assembler, ld, objdump, truss and gdb. By the end of the module you can read and write small assembly programs for both systems, call each operating system without a library, and follow one system call instruction by instruction. Module 5 builds on this to explain compilers, object files and executables, and Module 6 uses it for hardware interrupts and port I/O.

Francesco Valerio Buccoli · francesco@buccoli.com

Learning goals. After this module you can:

  • decode short sequences of 8086 and x86-64 machine code by hand (opcode, ModR/M byte, displacement, immediate, little-endian order) and check the result with DEBUG's U command, ndisasm and objdump -d;
  • name the registers and flags of the 8086 and of x86-64, and compute a real-mode address from a segment:offset pair;
  • read the same code in MASM, NASM and AT&T syntax, and explain what an assembler does with labels, directives and macros, using the macros of the MS-DOS kernel source as the example;
  • assemble, run, single-step and save a program with MS-DOS 4.00's DEBUG, scripted from a file, and do the same kind of inspection with gdb on FreeBSD;
  • explain PUSH, POP, CALL, RET and BP/RBP stack frames, and what INT n, IRET, syscall and sysret save and restore;
  • write programs that call the operating system directly (INT 21h functions 09h, 40h and 4Ch on MS-DOS; the write and exit system calls on FreeBSD), including error handling with the carry flag;
  • describe the machine state at program entry for a .COM file, an .EXE file and a static FreeBSD ELF program;
  • follow a FreeBSD write from the libsys stub into the kernel and back, and compare it with the path of an INT 21h call through MS-DOS 4.00.

Prerequisites.

  • Module 0 (00-lab.md): the MS-DOS 4.00 image with tools/dos_run.py, the 1988 toolchain with tools/dos_tools.py, and the FreeBSD 15.1 virtual machine (which has nasm and gdb). On your own computer you need nasm (it includes ndisasm) and GNU objdump from any recent binutils.
  • Module 1, section 1.1 (real mode and the BIOS boot contract) and Module 2, sections 2.1 and 2.2 (the INT 21h dispatcher and the FreeBSD system call path seen from the kernel). This module looks at the same paths from the instruction level and from the programmer's side, and links back instead of repeating them.
  • Hexadecimal and two's complement arithmetic; C at the level of pointers and arrays.

4.1 From bytes to instructions#

Fetch, decode, execute#

The processor keeps the address of the next instruction in a register: IP (instruction pointer) together with the code segment register CS on the 8086, and RIP on x86-64. Execution is a loop (Figure 4.1): fetch the bytes at that address; decode them, which tells the processor what the instruction does, which operands it has and how many bytes it occupies; advance the instruction pointer past it; execute it, which may read or write registers, memory and flags. A jump, call, return or interrupt changes the instruction pointer again during the execute step. Because the pointer has already moved, relative jump targets and RIP-relative addresses are measured from the end of the instruction, not from its start. Modern processors overlap and reorder this work, but the visible result is always as if one instruction ran after the other.

The parts of an instruction#

An x86 instruction is between 1 and 15 bytes long and is built from up to six parts. Only the opcode is always present.

Part Bytes What it holds
Prefixes 0-4 segment override (2E = CS:, 36 = SS:, 3E = DS:, 26 = ES:), F3 = REP, 66 = operand size; on x86-64 also a REX prefix (40-4F)
Opcode 1-3 the operation; some opcodes carry a register number in their low 3 bits (B8+r is MOV r16,imm16, B0+r is MOV r8,imm8)
ModR/M 0-1 which register and which register-or-memory operand
SIB 0-1 scale, index and base (32- and 64-bit addressing only)
Displacement 0, 1, 2 or 4 a constant added to an address
Immediate 0, 1, 2, 4 (8 for MOV r64,imm64) a constant operand

Multi-byte numbers are stored little-endian, least significant byte first: BC 00 7C is MOV SP,7C00h. The ModR/M byte splits into three fields, mod (bits 7-6), reg (bits 5-3) and r/m (bits 2-0). The reg field names a register (or, for some opcodes, extends the opcode); mod = 11 means r/m names a register too, any other mod means r/m describes a memory operand with no, an 8-bit or a 16-bit displacement. The register numbers are:

Number 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
16-bit register AX CX DX BX SP BP SI DI
8-bit register AL CL DL BL AH CH DH BH
Segment register ES CS SS DS
16-bit memory (r/m) [BX+SI] [BX+DI] [BP+SI] [BP+DI] [SI] [DI] [BP] (mod = 00: a 16-bit address) [BX]

Decoding real bytes#

Three short sequences from the course's systems show most of the rules. The first is the start of the boot sector on the lab floppy, written by MSBOOT (Module 1, section 1.3). Its source begins like this:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.1 – The first instruction of the MS-DOS boot sector is a jump over data (MSBOOT.ASM lines 86-104)Source ↗
        ORG     ORIGIN

DSKADR  =       1EH*4                   ;POINTER TO DRIVE PARAMETERS

Public $START
$START:
        JMP     START
;----------------------------------------------------------
;
;       THE FOLLOWING DATA CONFIGURES THE BOOT PROGRAM
;       FOR ANY TYPE OF DRIVE OR HARDFILE
;
;J.K. Extened_BPB

if ibmcopyright
          DB      "IBM  "
else
          DB      "MSDOS"
endif

On the disk the sector starts EB 3C 90 4D 53 44 4F 53 34 2E 30. EB is a short jump; the next byte is a signed 8-bit distance, counted from the end of the jump. The jump ends at 7C02h, so the target is 7C02h + 3Ch = 7C3Eh. 90 is NOP, an instruction that does nothing; MASM added it, for a reason section 4.3 explains. The bytes that follow are the text MSDOS4.0 and the disk parameters, which are data. A disassembler does not know that. Started at the first byte, it decodes the text as instructions:

Output 4.1 – The boot sector of the lab floppy disassembled from its first byte (ndisasm on the host)
$ ndisasm -o 0x7c00 msboot.bin | head -7
00007C00  EB3C              jmp 0x7c3e
00007C02  90                nop
00007C03  4D                dec bp
00007C04  53                push bx
00007C05  44                inc sp
00007C06  4F                dec di
00007C07  53                push bx

M, S, D, O are 4D, 53, 44, 4F, and those happen to be one-byte instructions. The processor never executes them, because the jump skips them. Code and data are both just bytes; only the path of execution decides which bytes are instructions. The jump lands on START:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.2 – MSBOOT sets up its stack (MSBOOT.ASM lines 145-168)Source ↗
START:

⋮
        CLI                             ;Stop interrupts till stack ok
        XOR     AX,AX
        MOV     SS,AX                   ;Work in stack just below this routine
        ASSUME  SS:CODE
        MOV     SP,ORIGIN
        PUSH    SS
        POP     ES
        ASSUME  ES:CODE
⋮
        MOV     BX,DSKADR
        LDS     SI,DWORD PTR SS:[BX]    ; get address of disk table
Output 4.2 – The same instructions in the boot sector (ndisasm on the host, starting at START)
$ ndisasm -o 0x7c3e -e 0x3e msboot.bin | head -8
00007C3E  FA                cli
00007C3F  33C0              xor ax,ax
00007C41  8ED0              mov ss,ax
00007C43  BC007C            mov sp,0x7c00
00007C46  16                push ss
00007C47  07                pop es
00007C48  BB7800            mov bx,0x78
00007C4B  36C537            lds si,word [ss:bx]

FreeBSD's boot0 (Module 1, section 1.2) starts with the same kind of set-up, written in AT&T syntax:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 4.3 – The first instructions of FreeBSD's boot0 (boot0.S lines 172-177)Source ↗
start:          cld                             # String ops inc
                xorw %ax,%ax                    # Zero
                movw %ax,%es                    # Address
                movw %ax,%ds                    #  data
                movw %ax,%ss                    # Set up
                movw $LOAD,%sp                  #  stack

The installed /boot/boot0 begins FC 31 C0 8E C0 8E D8 8E D0 BC 00 7C (Lab 4.1). Decoded by hand:

Bytes Fields Instruction
B4 09 opcode B0+4 (register 4 of the 8-bit set = AH), immediate 09 MOV AH,9
CD 21 opcode CD, immediate vector number 21 INT 21h
EB 3C opcode EB, 8-bit relative distance 3C JMP SHORT to (end of instruction) + 3Ch
FC opcode only CLD (clear the direction flag)
33 C0 opcode 33 = XOR r16, r/m16; ModR/M C0 = 11 000 000: reg = 0 (AX), mod = 11, r/m = 0 (AX) XOR AX,AX
31 C0 opcode 31 = XOR r/m16, r16; same ModR/M XOR AX,AX
8E D8 opcode 8E = MOV Sreg, r/m16; ModR/M D8 = 11 011 000: reg = 3 (DS), r/m = 0 (AX) MOV DS,AX
8E D0 ModR/M D0 = 11 010 000: reg = 2 (SS) MOV SS,AX
BC 00 7C opcode B8+4 (SP), 16-bit immediate 7C00, little-endian MOV SP,7C00h
36 C5 37 prefix 36 (SS:), opcode C5 = LDS; ModR/M 37 = 00 110 111: reg = 6 (SI), mod = 00, r/m = 7 ([BX]) LDS SI,SS:[BX]

33 C0 and 31 C0 are two encodings of the same instruction. For two register operands either operand can sit in the ModR/M r/m field, and bit 1 of the opcode says which one is the destination. MASM chose 33 for MSBOOT, while LLVM (which assembled boot0) and NASM choose 31. Such choices are fingerprints of the assembler that produced a binary.

The same bytes can also mean different things in different processor modes. In 64-bit mode 31 C0 is xor eax,eax, because the default operand size there is 32 bits, and the byte 48, which is DEC AX on the 8086, becomes a prefix that widens the next instruction to 64 bits. A disassembler therefore has to be told the mode: ndisasm -b 16 (the default) or -b 64, and objdump -m i8086 for 16-bit code. DEBUG only knows real mode.

Three tools turn bytes back into text: DEBUG's U (unassemble) command on MS-DOS, which reads memory; ndisasm, which reads a raw file of bytes and needs a starting address (-o) to compute jump targets; and objdump -d, which reads object and executable files (ELF on FreeBSD) and uses their symbol tables to label the code. GNU objdump on the host and LLVM objdump in the FreeBSD VM both print AT&T syntax by default. Lab 4.1 uses all three.

4.2 Registers and addresses#

The 8086 register file#

The 8086 has fourteen 16-bit registers (Figure 4.2). Four general registers can also be used as two 8-bit halves: AX is AH (high byte) and AL (low byte), and the same for BX, CX and DX. Most instructions accept any general register, but many give one register a special role, which is where the names come from:

Register Name Special roles
AX (AH, AL) accumulator MUL, DIV, IN, OUT; the INT 21h function number goes in AH
BX (BH, BL) base one of the two registers that can be the base of an address
CX (CH, CL) count LOOP, REP, JCXZ; shift counts in CL
DX (DH, DL) data high word of MUL and DIV; port number for IN and OUT
SI, DI source and destination index string instructions copy from DS:SI to ES:DI
BP base pointer the other address base; addresses the stack segment, so it is used for stack frames
SP stack pointer top of the stack, SS:SP
CS, DS, SS, ES segment registers code, data, stack and extra segment
IP instruction pointer the next instruction, CS:IP
FLAGS flags condition codes and control bits

The flags record properties of the last result (status flags) or control the processor (control flags). DEBUG prints them as two-letter names, and its table of names lists them in bit order:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.4 – DEBUG's names for the flag bits, from bit 15 down to bit 0 (DEBCONST.ASM lines 996-1032)Source ↗
; Flags are ordered to correspond with the bits of the flag
; register, most significant bit first, zero if bit is not
; a flag. First 16 entries are for bit set, second 16 for
; bit reset.

FLAGTAB    DW   0
           DW   0
           DW   0
           DW   0
           DB   "OV"
           DB   "DN"
           DB   "EI"                    ; "STI"
           DW   0
           DB   "NG"
           DB   "ZR"
           DW   0
           DB   "AC"
           DW   0
           DB   "PE"
           DW   0
           DB   "CY"
           DW   0
           DW   0
           DW   0
           DW   0
           DB   "NV"
           DB   "UP"                    ; "CLD"
           DB   "DI"
           DW   0
           DB   "PL"
           DB   "NZ"
           DW   0
           DB   "NA"
           DW   0
           DB   "PO"
           DW   0
           DB   "NC"
Bit Flag Set when DEBUG set / clear gdb name
11 OF overflow the signed result does not fit OV / NV OF
10 DF direction (control) string instructions count down DN / UP DF
9 IF interrupt enable (control) hardware interrupts are accepted EI / DI IF
8 TF trap (control) interrupt after each instruction not shown TF
7 SF sign the top bit of the result is 1 NG / PL SF
6 ZF zero the result is 0 ZR / NZ ZF
4 AF auxiliary carry a carry out of the low 4 bits (for BCD arithmetic) AC / NA AF
2 PF parity the low byte of the result has an even number of 1 bits PE / PO PF
0 CF carry an unsigned result does not fit (carry or borrow) CY / NC CF

Bit 8 has a zero entry in the table: DEBUG never shows the trap flag, because it uses that flag itself to execute your program one instruction at a time (section 4.4). Conditional jumps test these flags: JZ/JE tests ZF, JC/JB tests CF, JS tests SF, JO tests OF, and JL, JG and their relatives combine SF, OF and ZF for signed comparisons. CF matters beyond arithmetic: both systems in this course report system call errors in it (section 4.6).

Segment:offset addresses#

Module 2, section 2.1 gives the rule: a real-mode address is a 16-bit segment and a 16-bit offset, and the processor forms the 20-bit physical address as segment * 16 + offset (Figure 4.3). Some consequences matter when you program:

  • Many pairs name the same byte. 0040:0017 and 0000:0417 are both physical 00417h. The INT 21h entry point of our MS-DOS, 02C1:1716 (section 4.5), is physical 02C10h + 1716h = 04326h.
  • A segment is a 64 KB window that starts on a 16-byte paragraph boundary. A program that needs more than 64 KB of code or data must load different values into the segment registers, which is the subject of Module 5's memory models.
  • FFFF:FFFF would be 10FFEFh, beyond 1 MB; the 8086 wraps such addresses around to the start of memory.

An instruction usually does not name a segment register; the processor picks one by default:

Access Default segment
instruction fetch CS (with IP)
PUSH, POP, CALL, RET, INT, IRET SS (with SP)
memory operand whose address uses BP SS
any other memory operand DS
destination of a string instruction (STOSB, MOVSB) ES (with DI), cannot be overridden

A segment override prefix replaces the default for one instruction. MSBOOT's LDS SI,DWORD PTR SS:[BX] (Listing 4.2) assembles to 36 C5 37: without the 36 the processor would read through DS. DEBUG shows a prefix on a line of its own, as the CS: in the trace of Study case 4.A. The MS-DOS kernel uses CS: overrides often, because on entry to a system call DS still belongs to the caller while the kernel's own variables live in its code group.

The memory operands of 16-bit code are limited to the eight r/m forms in the table of the previous section, plus a displacement: one of BX or BP, one of SI or DI, both, or neither. MOV AX,[CX] cannot be encoded at all.

x86-64#

x86-64 extends the same design (Figure 4.2). There are sixteen 64-bit general registers: RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RBP, RSP and the new R8 to R15. Each has smaller views: EAX is the low 32 bits of RAX, AX the low 16 and AL the low 8 (AH still exists); R8D, R8W and R8B are the views of R8, and SIL, DIL, SPL and BPL are new 8-bit views. One rule surprises 8086 programmers: writing a 32-bit register clears the upper 32 bits of the 64-bit register, while writing an 8- or 16-bit view leaves the other bits alone. That is why compilers and the programs in this module write mov eax, 4 and xor eax, eax: the result is the same as with RAX, and the instruction is shorter.

A REX prefix (40-4F, binary 0100WRXB) reaches the new registers and the 64-bit size: W = 1 selects a 64-bit operand, and R, X and B add a fourth bit to the ModR/M reg field, the SIB index and the r/m or base field. 48 89 E5 is mov rbp, rsp, and 49 89 CA (W and B set) is mov r10, rcx, which appears in every FreeBSD system call stub (Lab 4.7). The instruction pointer is RIP, and RFLAGS keeps the 8086 flags in the same bit positions; gdb lists the set ones, for example [ CF PF IF ].

Segments are almost gone. In 64-bit mode the processor treats the bases of CS, DS, ES and SS as 0 and checks no limits; CS still selects 64-bit mode and the privilege level. Only FS and GS keep a base address, and FreeBSD uses FS for thread-local storage (pcb_fsbase in section 4.7). An address in a program is a 64-bit virtual address, which the page tables translate to a physical one (Module 2, section 2.5; Module 8). On amd64, user addresses lie below 0x0000800000000000, 128 TiB (arch(7)). The course VM's processor has 5-level paging and its kernel uses it (sysctl vm.pmap.la57 prints 1), which would allow 64 PiB, but arch(7) explains that processes still get the 48-bit layout by default, for compatibility (vm.pmap.prefer_uva_la48 is 1). The stacks in this module's FreeBSD outputs sit just below the 128 TiB limit, at 0x7fffffffxxxx.

Memory operands are general: [base + index * scale + displacement] with any registers, a scale of 1, 2, 4 or 8 and a 32-bit displacement. 64-bit mode adds RIP-relative addressing: the ModR/M combination that meant "32-bit absolute address" in 32-bit code means "RIP plus a 32-bit displacement". In Lab 4.6 the instruction lea rsi, [rel msg] becomes 48 8D 35 CF EF FF FF: REX.W, opcode 8D (LEA), ModR/M 35 = 00 110 101 (reg = 6, RSI; mod = 00 with r/m = 101, RIP-relative) and the displacement FFFFEFCF = -1031h. The next instruction starts at 201151h, and 201151h - 1031h = 200120h, the address of msg. Such code works wherever it is loaded, without the load-time fixups that the 8086 needs for segment values (Lab 4.3).

8086, real mode x86-64, 64-bit mode (FreeBSD programs)
General registers 8 of 16 bits 16 of 64 bits
Instruction pointer CS:IP RIP
Address segment * 16 + offset, 20 bits, physical 64-bit virtual, translated by page tables
Largest object without changing segment registers 64 KB the whole user address space (128 TiB)
Memory operand [BX or BP + SI or DI + disp16] [base + index * 1/2/4/8 + disp32], [RIP + disp32]
Protection none privilege levels and page permissions

4.3 Assemblers and their syntaxes#

What an assembler does#

An assembler translates one line of text into the bytes of one instruction, and it handles everything around the instructions that a person should not have to count by hand:

  • Labels. The assembler keeps a location counter, the offset of the next byte it will emit. A label such as START: gives the current value of the counter a name, and every use of the name becomes a number: the target of JMP START, the offset in MOV DX,OFFSET MSG.
  • Directives. Lines that emit no instruction but control the output: data (DB, DW in MASM; db, dw in NASM; .byte, .ascii in GNU syntax), constants (EQU, =), the origin of the location counter (ORG 100h in a .COM program, ORG 7C00h in a boot sector), sections or segments, and the entry point (END START).
  • Output. Either an object file with symbols and relocations, the places where an address can only be filled in later, by the linker or the loader, or a flat binary that is exactly the bytes, which is how boot sectors and .COM programs can be made with NASM (nasm -f bin). MASM writes Microsoft's OMF object format; NASM and clang write ELF on FreeBSD. Object formats, linking and relocation are the subject of Module 5.
  • Macros and conditional assembly. Named pieces of text with parameters, expanded before assembly, and IF/ENDIF blocks such as the if ibmcopyright in Listing 4.1. The MS-DOS source uses macros so heavily that they form a small language of their own (Study case 4.C).

Labels used before they are defined, forward references, are the classic difficulty. MASM 5.10 reads the source twice. In pass 1 it must decide how many bytes JMP START takes before it knows where START is, so it reserves three, enough for a near jump with a 16-bit distance. In pass 2 it knows the distance; if it fits in 8 bits it emits the 2-byte short jump and fills the third byte with NOP, because every later label already has its address from pass 1. That is the 90 after EB 3C at the start of the MS-DOS boot sector. The programmer can say JMP SHORT to get two bytes from the start:

Output 4.3 – MASM 5.10 listing of FWD.ASM (labs/04-asm/FWD.ASM), assembled with tools/dos_tools.py --dir work/04 "MASM FWD,,FWD;"
 0000                           CODE    SEGMENT
                                        ASSUME  CS:CODE
 0000  EB 0B 90                         JMP     AHEAD
 0003  000A[                            DB      10 DUP (0)
           00
                         ]

 000D  EB FE                    AHEAD:  JMP     AHEAD
 000F  EB 0A                            JMP     SHORT FAR1
 0011  000A[                            DB      10 DUP (0)
           00
                         ]

 001B  90                       FAR1:   NOP
 001C                           CODE    ENDS
                                        END

The backward jump JMP AHEAD at 000D needs no padding: its target is known, and EB FE (a distance of -2) is the shortest possible endless loop. NASM, the assembler used for the course's own MS-DOS programs, repeats its passes until the sizes stop changing and never pads.

Three syntaxes for one instruction set#

The instruction set is defined by Intel and AMD, but the way of writing it is defined by each assembler. This course meets three syntaxes:

MASM (MS-DOS source) NASM (both systems in this course) AT&T (FreeBSD source, cc, objdump, gdb)
Operand order destination, source: MOV AX,BX destination, source: mov ax, bx source, destination: movw %bx, %ax
Registers AX ax %ax
Constants 7C00h 7C00h or 0x7c00 $0x7c00
Memory operand WORD PTR [BX+SI+4], ES:[DI] word [bx+si+4], [es:di] 4(%bx,%si), %es:(%di)
x86-64 memory operand (none) [rdi + rcx*8 + 16], [rel msg] 16(%rdi,%rcx,8), msg(%rip)
Operand size from a register operand, or BYTE PTR, WORD PTR from a register operand, or byte, word, qword suffix b, w, l or q on the mnemonic
Address of a label OFFSET MSG (a plain MSG means the memory at MSG) msg (the memory is [msg]) $msg (a plain msg means the memory)
Comment ; ; #, or /* */ in .S files, which pass through the C preprocessor

The MASM rule in the second-last row causes many beginners' bugs: MASM remembers that MSG was defined with DB and treats the name as a variable, so the address must be asked for with OFFSET. NASM has no such memory; a name is always an address, and square brackets always mean memory.

The boot-sector set-up code of Listings 4.2 and 4.3 is a good test. The course provides it in all three syntaxes, labs/04-asm/SETUPM.ASM, labs/04-asm/setup.asm and labs/04-asm/freebsd/setup.S. The last one is written like boot0.S:

Example 4.1 – The set-up code in AT&T syntax (labs/04-asm/freebsd/setup.S)
/* setup.S - section 4.3: boot-sector set-up code in AT&T syntax (as in boot0.S) */
        .code16
        .text
start:  cld
        xorw    %ax, %ax
        movw    %ax, %es
        movw    %ax, %ds
        movw    %ax, %ss
        movw    $0x7c00, %sp

Assembled with the three assemblers, it gives the same twelve bytes except for the XOR:

Output 4.4 – The listing written by MASM 5.10 (MASM SETUPM,,SETUPM; with tools/dos_tools.py)
 0000                           CODE    SEGMENT
                                        ASSUME  CS:CODE
 0000  FC                       START:  CLD
 0001  33 C0                            XOR     AX,AX
 0003  8E C0                            MOV     ES,AX
 0005  8E D8                            MOV     DS,AX
 0007  8E D0                            MOV     SS,AX
 0009  BC 7C00                          MOV     SP,7C00h
 000C                           CODE    ENDS
                                        END     START
Output 4.5 – The listing written by NASM on the host (nasm -f bin -l setup.lst -o setup.bin setup.asm)
     3                                          bits    16
     4 00000000 FC                      start:  cld
     5 00000001 31C0                            xor     ax, ax
     6 00000003 8EC0                            mov     es, ax
     7 00000005 8ED8                            mov     ds, ax
     8 00000007 8ED0                            mov     ss, ax
     9 00000009 BC007C                          mov     sp, 7C00h
Output 4.6 – clang's assembler and LLVM objdump in the FreeBSD VM (captured in the course VM)
$ cc -c setup.S && objdump -d --triple=i386-unknown-unknown-code16 setup.o

setup.o:        file format elf64-x86-64

Disassembly of section .text:

0000000000000000 <start>:
       0: fc                            cld
       1: 31 c0                         xorw    %ax, %ax
       3: 8e c0                         movw    %ax, %es
       5: 8e d8                         movw    %ax, %ds
       7: 8e d0                         movw    %ax, %ss

Note how each tool prints the immediate of the last instruction: MASM's listing shows the 16-bit value 7C00, while NASM and objdump show the bytes in memory order, 00 7C. The ELF object file is a 64-bit object even though the code is 16-bit; objdump must be told the mode with --triple, or it decodes the bytes as 64-bit code (Exercise 4.1 asks you to try). The bytes of Output 4.6 are the first twelve bytes of the installed /boot/boot0, which Lab 4.1 dumps.

4.4 DEBUG: an assembler and debugger in one program#

A monitor in 21 KB#

DEBUG.COM is the oldest kind of debugger, a monitor: a small program that shows and changes memory and registers, and runs another program under control. The MS-DOS 4.00 version (v4.0/src/CMD/DEBUG, 21,574 bytes as built for the course) also contains a one-line-at-a-time assembler (A) and a disassembler (U), so with nothing but DEBUG you can write, run, inspect and save machine code. Every command is one letter, and the dispatcher is itself a lesson in assembly language: the letter, minus A, times two, is an index into a table of addresses.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.5 – DEBUG turns the command letter into an index and calls through a table (DEBUG.ASM lines 587-600)Source ↗
        LODSB                           ; AL=first non-blank character
; Prepare command letter for table lookup
; converts the first non-blank (assumed to be the command letter)
; to in index in the "comtab" array.
        SUB     AL,UPPER_A              ; Low end range check
        JB      ERR1

        CMP     AL,UPPER_Z - UPPER_A    ; Upper end range check
        JA      ERR1

        SHL     AL,1                    ; Times two
        CBW                             ; Now a 16-bit quantity
        XCHG    BX,AX                   ; In BX we can address with it
        CALL    CS:[BX+COMTAB]          ; Execute command

SUB sets the carry flag when the character is below A, so JB (jump if below, the same instruction as JC) rejects it; CBW widens AL to AX; and XCHG moves the index into BX, because BX can be used as an address base and AX cannot (section 4.2). The CALL is indirect: it reads its target from the word at CS:COMTAB + BX.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.6 – DEBUG's command table (DEBUG.ASM lines 1000-1032)Source ↗
; Command Table. Command letter indexes into table to get
; address of command. PERR prints error for no such command.

COMTAB  DW      ASSEM                   ; A
        DW      PERR                    ; B
        DW      COMPARE                 ; C
        DW      DUMP                    ; D
        DW      ENTERDATA               ; E
        DW      FILL                    ; F
        DW      GO                      ; G
        DW      HEXADD                  ; H
        DW      INPUT                   ; I
        DW      PERR                    ; J
        DW      PERR                    ; K
        DW      LOAD                    ; L
        DW      MOVE                    ; M
        DW      NAMED                   ; N
        DW      OUTPUT                  ; O
        DW      ZTRACE                  ; P
        DW      QUIT                    ; Q (QUIT)
        DW      REG                     ; R
        DW      SEARCH                  ; S
        DW      TRACE                   ; T
        DW      UNASSEM                 ; U
        DW      PERR                    ; V
        DW      DWRITE                  ; W
        IF      SYSVER
            DW      SETUDEV             ; X
        ELSE
            DW      DEBEMS
        ENDIF
        DW      PERR                    ; Y
        DW      PERR                    ; Z

The commands this module uses:

Command Meaning
A 100 assemble the lines that follow into memory from offset 100h, until an empty line
U 100 L C unassemble (disassemble) 0Ch bytes from offset 100h
D SS:FFE8 L 6 dump 6 bytes, as hexadecimal and as characters
E 200 B4 09 enter bytes into memory
R, R CX show all registers; show and change one register
T, T 5 trace: execute one (or five) instructions, showing the registers after each
P proceed: like T, but runs a CALL, INT, LOOP or REP instruction to its end
G 11A go: run until the instruction at offset 11Ah
N NAME.COM, L, W name a file, load it, write BX:CX bytes from offset 100h to it
Q quit

All numbers are hexadecimal, without an h. An address is an offset (in DS for D and E, in CS for A, U and G), or a segment:offset pair in which the segment may be a register name. Started as DEBUG HELLO.COM, DEBUG loads the program as EXEC would and stops before its first instruction; the R command then shows the registers a program receives (Lab 4.3):

Output 4.7 – The registers of a .COM program before its first instruction (MS-DOS 4.00, Lab 4.3)
-R

AX=0000  BX=0000  CX=0025  DX=0000  SP=FFFE  BP=0000  SI=0000  DI=0000
DS=1756  ES=1756  SS=1756  CS=1756  IP=0100   NV UP EI PL NZ NA PO NC
1756:0100 B409          MOV     AH,09

The first two lines are the register file of Figure 4.2 with the flags of Listing 4.4; the third is the next instruction, at CS:IP, with its bytes and its disassembly.

Scripting DEBUG#

On the lab machine nobody types at the keyboard, and you would not want to anyway: a script can be repeated and corrected. DEBUG reads its commands from standard input, so COMMAND.COM's input redirection (Module 3, section 3.4) turns a text file into a session: DEBUG <HELLO.SCR, or DEBUG HELLO.COM <RCOM.SCR to load a program first. Three rules make scripts work:

  1. The last command must be Q. At the end of the file DEBUG does not stop, it waits for more input, and dos_run.py ends the run only when its --timeout expires.
  2. An empty line ends the input of an A command.
  3. DEBUG echoes every command it reads, followed by an empty line, so the output can be read as a session.

How T, G and P work#

To execute one instruction of your program and then get control back, DEBUG uses the trap flag. It loads the program's registers, pushes the program's flags with TF set, its CS and its IP onto the program's stack, and executes IRET:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.7 – T sets the trap flag in the saved flags and returns into the program with IRET (DEBCOM3.ASM lines 268-324)Source ↗
CHECKOP:
        MOV     RSETFLAG,AL             ; no bits to turn off
SETTRACE:
        OR      FLSAVE,F_TRACE           ; Turn on trace bit
⋮
        PUSH    DS
        XOR     AX,AX
        MOV     DS,AX
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[12],OFFSET DG:BREAKFIX ; Set vector 3--breakpoint instruction
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[14],CS
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[4],OFFSET DG:REENTER ; Set vector 1--Single step
        MOV     WORD PTR DS:[6],CS
⋮
        POP     SS
        MOV     SP,[SPSAVE]
        PUSH    [FLSAVE]
        PUSH    [CSSAVE]
        PUSH    [IPSAVE]
        MOV     DS,[DSSAVE]
        IRET

IRET pops IP, CS and the flags in one instruction, so the processor continues in the program with TF set. After one instruction it raises interrupt 1, whose vector (at 0000:0004, four bytes per vector) now points to DEBUG's REENTER, which saves the registers and prints them. That is why DEBUG never shows TF: it is always set while the program runs and always clear when you look. The INT instruction needs special care: according to the comment in Listing 4.8, the 286 treats a software interrupt in trace mode as one atomic operation, so a traced INT would not stop at the first instruction of the handler. DEBUG therefore does what the processor would do itself, in software:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.8 – T simulates an INT instruction: read the vector, push flags, CS and IP, clear IF and TF (DEBCOM3.ASM lines 180-256)Source ↗
STEP:
        MOV     [BRKCNT],0
; The 286 has a problem with trace mode and software interrupt instructions;
; it treats them as atomic operations.  We simulate the operation in software.
        MOV     ES,[CSSAVE]             ; Get next instruction pointer
        MOV     DI,[IPSAVE]
        MOV     AL,ES:[DI]              ; get next opcode
⋮
not_mask_op:
        CMP     AL,0CDH                 ; trace over an interrupt?
        JZ      DOINT                   ; no, check for other special cases
⋮
DOINT:
; We have a software interrupt.  Get destination vector
        MOV     BL,BYTE PTR ES:[DI+1]   ; get vector number
        XOR     BH,BH                   ; clear out upper
DOVAL:
        SHL     BX,1                    ; word index
        SHL     BX,1                    ; dword index
        XOR     DI,DI                   ; interrupt table
        MOV     ES,DI
        MOV     AX,ES:[BX]              ; point to vector
        MOV     BX,ES:[BX+2]            ; point to vector
; AX:BX is the vector.  Swap it with currect CS:IP
        XCHG    AX,IPSAVE               ; new CS:IP
        XCHG    BX,CSSAVE
; AX:BX is old CS:IP.  We 'PUSH' flags, oldCS and oldIP, reset flags (ifl) and
; set CS:IP to point to interrupt instruction.
        MOV     ES,SSSAVE               ; point to user stack
        MOV     DI,SPSAVE
; Take old flags and PUSH the flags.
        MOV     CX,FLSAVE                ; get flags
        SUB     DI,2                    ; PUSHF
        MOV     ES:[DI],CX              ; rest of push
; Push the old CS
        SUB     DI,2                    ; PUSH CS
        MOV     ES:[DI],BX              ; rest of push
; Push the old IP
        SUB     DI,2                    ; PUSH IP
        ADD     AX,2                    ; increment IP
        MOV     ES:[DI],AX              ; rest of push
; Update stack
        MOV     SPSAVE,DI               ; store
; Take flags and turn interrupts off and trace mode off
        AND     CX,NOT F_INTERRUPT      ; CLI
        AND     CX,NOT F_TRACE          ; no trace
        MOV     FLSAVE,CX                ; rest of CLI

The block is a precise description of INT n on the 8086: the vector is the doubleword at 0000:n*4; the flags, CS and the address of the next instruction (IP + 2, because INT n is two bytes long) are pushed in that order; IF and TF are cleared; CS:IP is loaded from the vector. After T on an INT 21h you are therefore at the first instruction of the MS-DOS dispatcher, with the return address on the stack, which Study case 4.A uses.

G uses a different mechanism. For each breakpoint address it saves the original byte and writes CC there (DEBCOM3.ASM lines 600-604). CC is INT 3, the only one-byte INT instruction, so it fits over the first byte of any instruction. When the program reaches it, interrupt 3 enters DEBUG, which puts the original bytes back. P combines the two: if the next instruction is a CALL, INT, LOOP or REP string instruction, DEBUG computes its length from the opcode and the ModR/M byte, puts a single CC right after it and lets the program run:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.9 – P decodes the instruction length and plants one INT 3 after the instruction (DEBCOM3.ASM lines 92-156)Source ↗
        CMP     AL,11101000B            ; direct intra call
        JZ      ZTRACE3                 ; yes, 3 bytes
        CMP     AL,10011010B            ; direct inter call
        JZ      ZTRACE5                 ; yes, 5 bytes
        CMP     AL,11111111B            ; indirect?
        JZ      ZTRACEMODRM             ; yes, go figure length
        CMP     AL,11001100B            ; short interrupt?
        JZ      ZTRACE1                 ; yes, 1 byte
        CMP     AL,11001101B            ; long interrupt?
        JZ      ZTRACE2                 ; yes, 2 bytes
⋮
ZTRACE5:
        INC     DX
ZTRACE4:
        INC     DX
ZTRACE3:
        INC     DX
ZTRACE2:
        INC     DX
ZTRACE1:
        INC     DX
        ADD     DI,DX                   ; offset to breakpoint instruction
        MOV     WORD PTR [BPTAB],DI     ; save offset
        MOV     WORD PTR [BPTAB+2],ES   ; save segment
        MOV     AL,ES:[DI]              ; get next opcode byte
        MOV     BYTE PTR [BPTAB+4],AL   ; save it
        MOV     BYTE PTR ES:[DI],0CCH   ; break point it

The labels ZTRACE5 to ZTRACE1 fall through into each other, so jumping to ZTRACE3 adds 1 to DX three times: a compact way to turn "this instruction is three bytes long" into a number.

The same mechanisms on FreeBSD#

gdb on FreeBSD (Labs 4.7 and 4.8) offers the same services with different words: x/5i for U, x/8xb for D, info registers for R, stepi for T, nexti for P, break and continue for G. Underneath, the hardware mechanisms are the same: a breakpoint is an int3 byte (CC), written into the traced program's memory, and a single step is the trap flag. The difference is who does it. A FreeBSD process cannot touch another process's memory or registers; the debugger asks the kernel with the ptrace(2) system call, and the kernel sets the flag in the registers it saved for the traced thread:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 4.10 – FreeBSD single-steps a traced thread by setting PSL_T, the trap flag, in its saved flags (ptrace_machdep.c lines 409-419)Source ↗
int
ptrace_single_step(struct thread *td)
{

	PROC_LOCK_ASSERT(td->td_proc, MA_OWNED);
	if ((td->td_frame->tf_rflags & PSL_T) == 0) {
		td->td_frame->tf_rflags |= PSL_T;
		td->td_dbgflags |= TDB_STEP;
	}
	return (0);
}

td_frame->tf_rflags plays the role of DEBUG's FLSAVE: the flags that will be loaded when the thread returns to user mode. DEBUG can patch the interrupt vector table and other programs' memory because MS-DOS lets every program do so; on FreeBSD only the kernel can, and only for a debugger that is allowed to trace the target.

4.5 The stack, calls and interrupts#

The stack#

The stack is an area of ordinary memory that the processor manages with one register. On the 8086 it is the pair SS:SP, and SP points at the last word stored. PUSH AX first subtracts 2 from SP and then stores AX at SS:SP; POP AX loads the word at SS:SP and then adds 2. The stack therefore grows towards lower addresses. On x86-64 the register is RSP, SS plays no part, and PUSH and POP move 8 bytes. Nothing checks the limits: a program that pushes too much overwrites whatever lies below its stack, which on MS-DOS is usually its own code or data.

CALL and RET#

CALL target pushes the address of the next instruction, the return address, and jumps; RET pops that address into the instruction pointer. That is all the processor does. A far CALL on the 8086 pushes CS and then IP and loads both, and the matching far RET (RETF) pops both; RET n also adds n to SP after popping, which removes n bytes of arguments. Everything else, where the arguments go, which register holds the result, which registers a function may destroy, is a calling convention, an agreement between the programmer, the compiler and the libraries:

MS-DOS, Microsoft C 5.10 (cdecl, small model) FreeBSD amd64 (System V ABI)
Arguments pushed on the stack, last argument first RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9, then the stack
Who removes stack arguments the caller (ADD SP,4) the caller
Result AX, or DX:AX for 32 bits RAX, or RDX:RAX for 128 bits
Registers the function must preserve SI, DI, BP (and the segment registers DS, SS) RBX, RBP, R12-R15 (and RSP)
Stack alignment 2 bytes RSP is a multiple of 16 at every CALL
Below the stack pointer nothing may be stored a 128-byte red zone that a function may use without moving RSP

Module 5 compares the conventions with the compilers' own output. What matters here is the stack frame that a function builds with them (Figure 4.4). The classic 8086 prologue is PUSH BP and MOV BP,SP. After it, [BP] holds the caller's BP, [BP+2] the return address, [BP+4] the first argument and [BP+6] the second; local variables are reserved below with SUB SP,n and addressed as [BP-2], [BP-4]. BP stays fixed while SP moves, and because BP addresses the stack segment by default (section 4.2) no segment prefix is needed. The epilogue MOV SP,BP, POP BP, RET undoes it. The x86-64 version is the same with RBP, except that the arguments arrive in registers. Many compilers omit the frame pointer when they optimise and address everything relative to RSP; FreeBSD's cc keeps it on amd64 even with -O2, so that debuggers and profilers can walk the stack (Lab 4.8 shows pushq %rbp in compiled code). Lab 4.8 writes the same function, sum, for both machines and looks at the frames with DEBUG and gdb.

INT and IRET#

INT n is a call through a table. The 8086 keeps 256 interrupt vectors, each a segment:offset pair of 4 bytes, in the first kilobyte of memory: the vector for INT n is at physical address n * 4. INT n pushes the flags, CS and IP (of the next instruction), clears IF and TF, and loads CS:IP from the vector; IRET pops IP, CS and the flags. Listing 4.8 shows the same steps done in software by DEBUG. Because the flags are saved and restored, the handler can enable interrupts or change flags without affecting the caller, except where it deliberately writes into the saved flags on the stack, which is how MS-DOS returns the carry flag from INT 21h (Module 2, section 2.2.3). Hardware interrupts and exceptions use the same table and the same frame (Module 6).

The vectors of our MS-DOS can be read with DEBUG. Vector 20h is at 0000:0080:

Output 4.8 – The vectors of INT 20h to INT 23h, read with DEBUG (MS-DOS 4.00, labs/04-asm/INTSTEP.SCR)
-D 0:80 L 10

0000:0080  F5 16 C1 02 16 17 C1 02-FA 02 15 12 35 03 15 12   ............5...

Read as little-endian offset and segment, INT 20h ("terminate") points to 02C1:16F5 and INT 21h to 02C1:1716. The MS-DOS link map, MSDOS.MAP in the course's build, puts QUIT at 16F5 and COMMAND, the entry of the INT 21h dispatcher of Module 2, at 1716 in the kernel's code group, which was loaded at segment 02C1. INT 22h and INT 23h, the terminate address and the Ctrl-C handler, point into DEBUG itself (segment 1215), which installs both (DEBUG.ASM lines 393-397 and lines 606-612). Tracing an INT 21h with T then shows the frame that INT builds:

Output 4.9 – One T over INT 21h and the three words it pushed (MS-DOS 4.00, labs/04-asm/INTSTEP.SCR)
-T


AX=3000  BX=0000  CX=0000  DX=0000  SP=FFEE  BP=0000  SI=0000  DI=0000
DS=1741  ES=1741  SS=1741  CS=1741  IP=0102   NV UP EI PL NZ NA PO NC
1741:0102 CD21          INT     21
-T


AX=3000  BX=0000  CX=0000  DX=0000  SP=FFE8  BP=0000  SI=0000  DI=0000
DS=1741  ES=1741  SS=1741  CS=02C1  IP=1716   NV UP DI PL NZ NA PO NC
02C1:1716 2E            CS:
02C1:1717 3A26BC0E      CMP     AH,[0EBC]                          CS:0EBC=6C
-D SS:FFE8 L 6

1741:FFE0                          04 01 41 17 02 72                 ..A..r

SP dropped by 6, from FFEE to FFE8. The three words are IP = 0104 (the instruction after the 2-byte INT 21), CS = 1741 and the flags 7202: IF (bit 9) set, as it was before the INT. In the new state IF is clear (DI), and CS:IP is the vector. The upper bits 7000 are left over from DEBUG's initial flags word, F202h (DEBCONST.ASM line 1054): the emulated Pentium-class processor kept bits 12 to 14 (IOPL and NT) when the first T loaded that word, and cleared bit 15. They have no meaning in real mode. The first instruction of MS-DOS uses a CS: prefix, because DS still belongs to the caller; it compares the function number in AH with MAXCOM, the highest valid one, 6Ch (Module 2, section 2.2.2).

SYSCALL and SYSRET#

In 64-bit mode interrupts and exceptions still go through a table, now of 16-byte gates, and push a fixed frame of five 8-byte words (SS, RSP, RFLAGS, CS, RIP, plus an error code for some exceptions) on a kernel stack (Module 6). System calls use a faster pair of instructions instead. syscall does not touch memory at all: it copies RIP into RCX and RFLAGS into R11, masks some flags, switches to privilege level 0 and jumps to an address that the kernel stored in a model-specific register at boot. sysret copies RCX back into RIP and R11 into RFLAGS and returns to user mode. Because nothing was pushed, the kernel's first instructions must find a stack themselves. Module 2, Listing 2.11 shows them (fast_syscall in exception.S lines 525-536); read now at the instruction level, they do this:

  1. swapgs exchanges the user's GS base with the kernel's, which points at this processor's private data (PCPU). Without it the kernel could not find anything, because every general register still holds a user value.
  2. movq %rsp,PCPU(SCRATCH_RSP) parks the user's stack pointer there, and movq PCPU(RSP0),%rsp loads the kernel stack of the current thread.
  3. subq $TF_SIZE,%rsp reserves a trapframe, the same structure an interrupt would have filled, and the following movq instructions fill it by hand: the saved flags from R11, the return address from RCX, the user's RSP from the scratch slot, then the argument registers.

Two consequences reach every assembly programmer on FreeBSD: a system call destroys RCX and R11, and the fourth argument of a system call, which the C convention passes in RCX, must travel in R10 instead (the comment "%rcx original value is in %r10" on line 534). Figure 4.5 sets the two entry mechanisms side by side; section 4.6 and Study case 4.B follow them through.

4.6 System calls from assembly language#

MS-DOS: INT 21h#

Module 2, sections 2.2.1 to 2.2.3 describe the INT 21h convention from the kernel's side. For the programmer it comes down to a few rules: the function number goes in AH; the arguments go in the other registers, a buffer or file name usually in DS:DX; the dispatcher saves all registers on the caller's stack and restores them, except AL, which it takes from the function (Study case 4.A), so only AL and the documented result registers change; and the handle-based functions introduced with MS-DOS 2.0 report failure by setting the carry flag and putting an error code in AX. The older functions inherited from CP/M do not use the carry flag: the FCB file functions return 0 or FFh in AL (MS_CODE.ASM lines 312-322), and the character functions report nothing. This module uses:

AH Function Arguments Results
02h write the character in DL to standard output DL none
09h write a string ending in $ to standard output DS:DX none
30h get the MS-DOS version none AL = major, AH = minor version
3Fh read from a handle BX = handle, CX = count, DS:DX = buffer AX = bytes read (0 at end of file); CF and AX on error
40h write to a handle BX = handle, CX = count, DS:DX = buffer AX = bytes written; CF and AX on error
4Ch end the program AL = exit code does not return

Function 09h shows what a "system call" of MS-DOS is like inside: a loop of ordinary instructions.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.11 – Function 09h: load a byte, stop at $, output it, repeat (CPMIO.ASM lines 209-227)Source ↗
        procedure   $STD_CON_STRING_OUTPUT,NEAR   ;System call 9
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING

        MOV     SI,DX
STRING_OUT1:
        LODSB
⋮
        CMP     AL,'$'
        retz
NEXT_STR1:
        invoke  OUTT
        JMP     STRING_OUT1

ASSUME DS:NOTHING tells MASM that DS holds no known segment here: it is still the caller's DS, so LODSB (load the byte at DS:SI into AL and increment SI) reads the caller's string. retz and invoke are macros of the MS-DOS source, a conditional return and a call (Study case 4.C). OUTT handles tabs and control characters and finally calls RAWOUT, which writes the character to handle 1 (CPMIO.ASM lines 339-345), so even function 09h follows a redirection of standard output (Lab 4.2). What 09h cannot do is write a $, write to standard error, or write a string whose length is known but whose end is not marked. Function 40h can, which is why the course's MS-DOS programs use it:

Example 4.2 – Writing to handles 1 and 2 and returning an exit code on MS-DOS (labs/04-asm/hello4.asm)
; hello4.asm - Lab 4.4: NASM, handles and an exit code (MS-DOS .COM)
; nasm -f bin -o HELLO4.COM hello4.asm
        cpu     8086
        org     100h                    ; .COM: loaded at offset 100h

        mov     ah, 40h                 ; INT 21h 40h: write to a handle
        mov     bx, 1                   ; handle 1: standard output
        mov     cx, msglen              ; byte count, so '$' is allowed
        mov     dx, msg                 ; DS:DX -> the bytes
        int     21h
        jc      fail                    ; CF=1: AX holds an error code
        mov     ah, 40h
        mov     bx, 2                   ; handle 2: standard error
        mov     cx, errlen
        mov     dx, err
        int     21h
        mov     ax, 4C03h               ; 4Ch: exit, AL = exit code 3
        int     21h
fail:   mov     ah, 4Ch                 ; exit code = DOS error code
        int     21h

msg     db      'Price: $5, on handle 1', 13, 10
msglen  equ     $ - msg
err     db      'A note on handle 2', 13, 10
errlen  equ     $ - err

cpu 8086 makes NASM reject any instruction the 8086 does not have. msglen equ $ - msg lets the assembler count the bytes: $ is NASM's location counter, so the difference is the length of the text. On the error path AH is overwritten with 4Ch, but AL still holds the low byte of the error code, which becomes the exit code. Lab 4.4 runs the program and tests the code with IF ERRORLEVEL.

FreeBSD: the syscall instruction#

On FreeBSD a program asks the kernel for service with the syscall instruction, and the registers are:

MS-DOS 4.00, INT 21h FreeBSD 15.1 amd64, syscall
Function number AH (sometimes AL too: 4400h) RAX
Arguments BX, CX, DX, DS, SI, DI, ES, depending on the function RDI, RSI, RDX, R10, R8, R9, in that order
Result registers listed for each function RAX (and RDX)
Failure CF = 1, error code in AX CF = 1, errno value in RAX
Registers changed only the result registers and AL RAX, RDX, RCX, R11; R8-R10 may be cleared

The numbers come from the kernel's table, syscalls.master (Module 2, section 2.2.5), from which the build generates a header:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 4.12 – The first system call numbers (syscall.h lines 1-16)Source ↗
/*
 * System call numbers.
 *
 * DO NOT EDIT-- this file is automatically @generated.
 */

#define 	SYS_exit	SYS__exit

#define	SYS_syscall	0
#define	SYS__exit	1
#define	SYS_fork	2
#define	SYS_read	3
#define	SYS_write	4
#define	SYS_open	5
#define	SYS_close	6
#define	SYS_wait4	7

The argument order is not arbitrary. The kernel saves the user registers in a struct trapframe whose first six fields are exactly the six argument registers:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 4.13 – The saved user registers, arranged so that the system call arguments come first (frame.h lines 113-155)Source ↗
/*
 * Exception/Trap Stack Frame
 *
 * The ordering of this is specifically so that we can take first 6
 * the syscall arguments directly from the beginning of the frame.
 */

struct trapframe {
	register_t	tf_rdi;
	register_t	tf_rsi;
	register_t	tf_rdx;
	register_t	tf_rcx;
	register_t	tf_r8;
	register_t	tf_r9;
	register_t	tf_rax;
⋮
	/* below portion defined in hardware */
	register_t	tf_err;
	register_t	tf_rip;
	uint16_t	tf_cs;
	uint16_t	tf_fred_evinfo3;
	uint32_t	tf_fred_zero2;
	register_t	tf_rflags;
	/* the amd64 frame always has the stack registers */
	register_t	tf_rsp;
	uint16_t	tf_ss;
	uint16_t	tf_fred_evinfo1;
	uint32_t	tf_fred_evinfo2;
};

The entry code stores the user's R10 into tf_rcx (section 4.5), so the six arguments lie in order at the start of the frame and cpu_fetch_syscall_args copies them with one memcpy (trap.c lines 1132-1164, Module 2). The fields "defined in hardware" are the five words an interrupt pushes, plus the error code that some exceptions push, in the order in which they lie on the stack: tf_ss, pushed first, is at the highest address. On the way out, cpu_set_syscall_retval puts the result in tf_rax and clears the carry bit in tf_rflags, or puts the error number in tf_rax and sets the carry bit (Module 2, Listing 2.13): the same idea as MS-DOS, which sets the carry bit in the flags word that INT 21h pushed. A program written in assembly language does the same as hello4.asm:

Example 4.3 – Writing to standard output and exiting on FreeBSD (labs/04-asm/freebsd/hello.asm)
; hello.asm - Lab 4.6: hello on FreeBSD/amd64 with two system calls, NASM syntax
; nasm -f elf64 hello.asm && ld -o hello hello.o
        section .rodata
msg:    db      "Hello from x86-64 assembly", 10
len     equ     $ - msg

        section .text
        global  _start
_start: mov     eax, 4                  ; SYS_write
        mov     edi, 1                  ; fd 1: standard output
        lea     rsi, [rel msg]          ; buffer, RIP-relative
        mov     edx, len                ; byte count
        syscall                         ; RCX and R11 are overwritten
        jc      fail                    ; CF=1: RAX holds an errno value
        mov     eax, 1                  ; SYS_exit
        xor     edi, edi                ; status 0
        syscall                         ; does not return
fail:   mov     edi, eax                ; exit status = errno
        mov     eax, 1                  ; SYS_exit
        syscall

Line by line it is the MS-DOS program translated: the function number into the accumulator, the handle and the buffer into the argument registers, the system call instruction, a jc to the error path, and an exit with a status. The C library does the same in its system call stubs, plus one step: on failure it copies RAX into errno and returns -1 (Module 2, Listings 2.9 and 2.10). Lab 4.7 disassembles the real stub for write.

4.7 Where a program starts#

Every program begins with a machine state that someone else prepared: the registers, the stack and the memory layout at its first instruction. A program written in assembly language without a run-time library sees that state directly, so it must know it. Module 2, section 2.6 follows EXEC and execve through the kernel, Module 5 explains the file formats and the start-up code of C programs, and Module 9 reads the arguments. This section only collects the register-level facts.

.COM programs#

A .COM file is a memory image without a header. EXEC builds a 256-byte Program Segment Prefix (PSP), copies the file right after it, at offset 100h, and starts the program with all four segment registers equal to the PSP segment, IP = 100h and SP at the top of the 64 KB segment, below a word of zero pushed for it (Module 5, Listing 5.6, and Module 9, Listing 9.14, show the code). Output 4.7 is that state as DEBUG shows it. The zero word has a purpose. If the program ends with a plain RET, RET pops 0 into IP, and at PSP:0000 EXEC placed the bytes CD 20, INT 20h, the old CP/M-style "terminate" call (Lab 4.3 dumps both). The general registers are not part of the contract: AX reports whether the drive letters of the first two command-line arguments are valid (FF in AL or AH if not; EXEC.ASM lines 729-743), and the values of BX and CX that DEBUG shows (the file size) are set by DEBUG, so that W can write the program back, not by EXEC.

EXEC enters the program in an unusual way. It switches to the new stack, pushes the entry point's segment and offset, and executes RET inside a procedure declared FAR (EXEC.ASM lines 778-806). MASM assembles a RET in a FAR procedure as a far return, CB, which pops IP and CS: a "return" to an address that was never called, and the simplest way on the 8086 to jump to a segment:offset held in registers.

.EXE programs#

An .EXE file starts with a header that gives the initial CS:IP and SS:SP relative to the start of the program, plus a list of places that contain segment values (Module 5). EXEC loads the program after the PSP, adds the load segment to the initial CS and SS and to every listed place, and starts it with DS and ES still pointing at the PSP. Lab 4.3 builds the same program both ways and shows the difference:

Output 4.10 – The registers of the .EXE version before its first instruction (MS-DOS 4.00, Lab 4.3)
-R

AX=0000  BX=0000  CX=0039  DX=0000  SP=0100  BP=0000  SI=0000  DI=0000
DS=1756  ES=1756  SS=176A  CS=1766  IP=0000   NV UP EI PL NZ NA PO NC
1766:0000 B86817        MOV     AX,1768

The PSP is at 1756, and the program image starts 10h paragraphs (256 bytes) later, at 1766. The CODE segment is first, so CS = 1766; DATA starts 20h bytes into the image, so its segment is 1768; STACK starts at 40h, so SS = 176A, with SP = 0100 at the top of its 256 bytes. The first instruction, MOV AX,DATA in the source, has become MOV AX,1768: in the file it holds the segment value relative to the image, and EXEC added 1766 at load time. The program must still set DS itself, which is why every .EXE program written in assembly language begins with MOV AX,DATA and MOV DS,AX.

FreeBSD ELF programs#

On FreeBSD, execve maps the program's segments at the virtual addresses in its ELF header (Module 5), builds the new stack (Module 9, section 9.1) and then resets the thread's saved registers:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 4.14 – The registers of a new amd64 program (exec_machdep.c lines 425-443)Source ↗
	update_pcb_bases(pcb);
	pcb->pcb_fsbase = pcb->pcb_tlsbase = 0;
	pcb->pcb_gsbase = 0;
	clear_pcb_flags(pcb, PCB_32BIT | PCB_TLSBASE);
	pcb->pcb_initial_fpucw = __INITIAL_FPUCW__;

	saved_rflags = regs->tf_rflags & PSL_T;
	bzero((char *)regs, sizeof(struct trapframe));
	regs->tf_rip = imgp->entry_addr;
	regs->tf_rsp = ((stack - 8) & ~0xFul) + 8;
	regs->tf_rdi = stack;		/* argv */
	regs->tf_rflags = PSL_USER | saved_rflags;
	regs->tf_ss = _udatasel;
	regs->tf_cs = _ucodesel;
	regs->tf_ds = _udatasel;
	regs->tf_es = _udatasel;
	regs->tf_fs = _ufssel;
	regs->tf_gs = _ugssel;
	regs->tf_flags = TF_HASSEGS;

bzero clears the whole trapframe of Listing 4.13, so every general register starts at zero except the two that are set: RDI points at the argument count on the stack, and RSP is the same address, moved down by 8 if necessary so that the program starts with the stack alignment that a function would see after a CALL (section 4.5). Only the trap flag survives, so that a debugger can step from the very first instruction. The FS and GS bases are cleared; the C library or the run-time linker sets FS up for thread-local storage later. gdb shows the result for hello from Example 4.3, stopped before its first instruction:

At RSP lie argc (3), the three argv pointers, a zero, the environment pointers (the second variable, PWD, was added by the shell through which gdb starts the program) and, after another zero, the auxiliary vector, a list of number-value pairs in which the kernel tells the program about itself and the system. Here RSP and RDI are equal because the address was already aligned. EFLAGS holds only IF and the always-set bit 1. The two systems agree on the essentials: the kernel decides the entry point and the stack, and almost every other register starts with a value the program must not rely on, zero on FreeBSD, whatever EXEC and the previous program left on MS-DOS.

Labs#

The MS-DOS labs use a working copy of labs/04-asm, for example work/04, and the course tools from the repository root: dos_tools.py runs MASM 5.10 and LINK in DOSBox-X's own DOS with your directory as drive D:, and dos_run.py runs programs and DEBUG scripts on the MS-DOS 4.00 we built (always give it a --timeout). .COM programs written for NASM are assembled on the host with nasm -f bin. Script files for DEBUG (.SCR) and all MS-DOS sources keep CR LF line ends; do not let an editor convert them. The FreeBSD labs run in the course VM in ~/lab/04. Copy the lab files there once:

Terminal
$ tar -cf work/04/fbsd.tar -C labs/04-asm/freebsd .
$ python tools/bsd_run.py --put work/04/fbsd.tar:/root/lab/fbsd.tar "mkdir -p 04 && tar -xf fbsd.tar -C 04 && rm fbsd.tar"

FreeBSD commands are shown as $ command, run in ~/lab/04: type them in an SSH session (python tools/bsd_run.py --shell) or pass each one as "cd 04 && command" to bsd_run.py, which is how the outputs below were captured.

Lab 4.1: Decode bytes by hand, then check#

Goal. Decode real machine code by hand, then compare your result with three disassemblers.

What you need. labs/04-asm/DECODE.SCR, the lab floppy image build/images/dos400.img (Module 0), ndisasm on the host, the FreeBSD VM.

Steps.

  1. On paper, decode EB 3C 90, B4 09 CD 21 and FC 31 C0 8E C0 8E D8 8E D0 BC 00 7C with the tables of section 4.1. Write the instruction, its length and, for each ModR/M byte, the three fields in binary.

  2. Check with DEBUG on MS-DOS 4.00. The script loads sector 0 of drive A (L 100 0 0 1: to offset 100h, drive 0, sector 0, one sector), dumps and unassembles it, then enters your byte sequences with E and unassembles them:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 60 --file A:\DECODE.SCR=work/04/DECODE.SCR "DEBUG <DECODE.SCR"

  3. On the host, cut the boot sector out of the image and disassemble it twice, from its first byte and from START (Outputs 4.1 and 4.2):

    Terminal
    $ python -c "open('work/04/msboot.bin','wb').write(open('build/images/dos400.img','rb').read(512))"
$ ndisasm -o 0x7c00 work/04/msboot.bin | head -7
$ ndisasm -o 0x7c3e -e 0x3e work/04/msboot.bin | head -8

  4. In the VM, dump and disassemble FreeBSD's boot0:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/bsd_run.py "ls -l /boot/boot0" "od -A x -t x1 -N 16 /boot/boot0" "ndisasm -o 0x7c00 /boot/boot0 | head -6"

What you should see.

$ ls -l /boot/boot0
-r--r--r--  1 root wheel 512 Jun 12 10:29 /boot/boot0
$ od -A x -t x1 -N 16 /boot/boot0
0000000    fc  31  c0  8e  c0  8e  d8  8e  d0  bc  00  7c  89  e6  bf  00
0000010
$ ndisasm -o 0x7c00 /boot/boot0 | head -6
00007C00  FC                cld
00007C01  31C0              xor ax,ax
00007C03  8EC0              mov es,ax
00007C05  8ED8              mov ds,ax
00007C07  8ED0              mov ss,ax
00007C09  BC007C            mov sp,0x7c00

What is going on. The same two bytes EB 3C are JMP 013E in DEBUG and jmp 0x7c3e in ndisasm. A short jump stores only the distance, +3Ch from the end of the instruction; DEBUG loaded the sector at offset 100h, ndisasm was told it lives at 7C00h, and each adds the distance to its own address. Code built from relative jumps runs wherever it is loaded. DEBUG's U 100 L 3 was told to stop after the NOP; if you unassemble further you get Output 4.1's nonsense, because U cannot tell code from data either. The two XOR AX,AX encodings, 33 C0 in the MASM-built MS-DOS sector and 31 C0 in the LLVM-built boot0 and in your hand-entered copy, are decoded to the same instruction by every tool.

Questions.

  1. BB 78 00 loads 78h into BX, and the next instruction is 36 C5 37. What lies at physical address 78h, and why does MSBOOT need the SS: prefix there (Listing 4.1 gives a hint)?
  2. Disassemble /boot/boot0 from offset 1 instead of 0 (ndisasm -o 0x7c01 -e 1). How many instructions does it take until the output agrees with Output 4.13 again?
  3. Which bytes would encode MOV DS,BX, MOV ES,AX and XOR SI,SI? Enter them with E and check with U.

Lab 4.2: Hello, world typed into DEBUG#

Goal. Write, run and save a program with nothing but MS-DOS 4.00's own DEBUG.

What you need. labs/04-asm/HELLO.SCR, tools/dos_run.py.

Steps.

  1. Read the script. N names the file, A 100 assembles at offset 100h (where a .COM program starts), the empty line ends the assembly, U and D show the result, RCX sets the length to write, W writes it:

    Example 4.4 – A DEBUG script that assembles and saves HELLO.COM (labs/04-asm/HELLO.SCR)
    N HELLO.COM
A 100
MOV AH,9
MOV DX,10C
INT 21
MOV AX,4C00
INT 21
DB "Hello from DEBUG",D,A,"$"

U 100 L C
D 100 L 20
RCX
1F
W
Q

  2. Run it, then run the new program, once on the screen and once redirected:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 60 --file A:\HELLO.SCR=work/04/HELLO.SCR "DEBUG <HELLO.SCR" "DIR HELLO.COM" "HELLO" "HELLO >H.TXT" "DIR H.TXT"

What is going on. DEBUG's assembler has no labels: it translates one line at a time, so the address of the message, 10C, had to be worked out before typing MOV DX,10C (2 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 12 bytes of code). The prompt before each line shows the location counter, which confirms the count: the DB line starts at 010C. W writes BX:CX bytes, starting at offset 100h, so RCX with 1F (31) makes the file exactly as long as code and text; the byte 8B after the $ in the dump is left over in memory and is not saved. The bytes match the decode table of section 4.1, B4 09 and CD 21 included. The redirected run writes 18 bytes, 16 characters plus CR and LF, into H.TXT: function 09h writes through handle 1 (section 4.6), and COMMAND.COM pointed handle 1 at the file.

Questions.

  1. You want to add MOV BX,1 before MOV DX,10C. Which other line of the script must change, and why would an assembler with labels not need that change?
  2. What would HELLO.COM contain if you had typed RCX 20 instead of 1F? Would the program still work?
  3. INT 20h also ends a .COM program. Rewrite the script to use it; how long is the file now, and where is the message?

Lab 4.3: The same program with MASM 5.10, as .COM and as .EXE#

Goal. Build one program as a .COM and as an .EXE with the 1988 assembler and linker, and compare the registers each one starts with (section 4.7).

What you need. labs/04-asm/HELLOC.ASM, HELLOE.ASM, RCOM.SCR, REXE.SCR, tools/dos_tools.py, tools/dos_run.py. Module 5 explains object files, LINK and the .EXE header in depth; here we only need the result.

Steps.

  1. Read the two sources. The .COM version has one segment and starts at ORG 100h; the .EXE version has separate code, data and stack segments and must load DS itself:

    Example 4.5 – labs/04-asm/HELLOC.ASM
            PAGE    ,132
; HELLOC.ASM - Lab 4.3: "hello" as a .COM program, MASM 5.10 syntax
; Build: MASM HELLOC;  LINK HELLOC;  EXE2BIN HELLOC HELLOC.COM
CODE    SEGMENT
        ASSUME  CS:CODE,DS:CODE
        ORG     100h            ; the first 256 bytes are the PSP
START:  MOV     AH,9            ; INT 21h function 09h: print string
        MOV     DX,OFFSET MSG   ; DS:DX -> text ending in '$'
        INT     21h
        MOV     AX,4C00h        ; function 4Ch: exit with code 0
        INT     21h
MSG     DB      'Hello from MASM (.COM)',13,10,'$'
CODE    ENDS
        END     START           ; entry point
    Example 4.6 – labs/04-asm/HELLOE.ASM
            PAGE    ,132
; HELLOE.ASM - Lab 4.3: the same program as an .EXE, MASM 5.10 syntax
; Build: MASM HELLOE;  LINK HELLOE;
CODE    SEGMENT PARA PUBLIC 'CODE'
        ASSUME  CS:CODE,DS:DATA,SS:STACK
MAIN    PROC    FAR
        MOV     AX,DATA         ; paragraph of DATA: a relocation,
        MOV     DS,AX           ;   fixed up by EXEC at load time
        MOV     AH,9            ; INT 21h function 09h: print string
        MOV     DX,OFFSET MSG   ; DS:DX -> text ending in '$'
        INT     21h
        MOV     AX,4C00h        ; function 4Ch: exit with code 0
        INT     21h
MAIN    ENDP
CODE    ENDS

DATA    SEGMENT PARA PUBLIC 'DATA'
MSG     DB      'Hello from MASM (.EXE)',13,10,'$'
DATA    ENDS

STACK   SEGMENT PARA STACK 'STACK'
        DW      128 DUP (?)     ; 256 bytes of stack
STACK   ENDS
        END     MAIN            ; entry point

  2. Assemble and link both (the ,, asks MASM for a listing file, LINK HELLOE,,HELLOE; for a map file):

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_tools.py --timeout 120 --dir work/04 "MASM HELLOC,,;" "LINK HELLOC;" "EXE2BIN HELLOC HELLOC.COM" "MASM HELLOE,,;" "LINK HELLOE,,HELLOE;" "DIR HELLO*.*"

  3. Run both programs on MS-DOS 4.00, then load each into DEBUG and look at the registers, at the word on top of the .COM program's stack and at the first bytes of its PSP. RCOM.SCR contains R, D SS:FFFE L 2, U CS:0 L 2, Q; REXE.SCR contains R, U CS:0 L 11, D CS:20 L 19, Q:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 60 --file A:\HELLOC.COM=work/04/HELLOC.COM --file A:\HELLOE.EXE=work/04/HELLOE.EXE --file A:\RCOM.SCR=work/04/RCOM.SCR --file A:\REXE.SCR=work/04/REXE.SCR "HELLOC" "HELLOE" "DEBUG HELLOC.COM <RCOM.SCR" "DEBUG HELLOE.EXE <REXE.SCR"

1766:000F CD21          INT     21
-D CS:20 L 19

1766:0020  48 65 6C 6C 6F 20 66 72-6F 6D 20 4D 41 53 4D 20   Hello from MASM
1766:0030  28 2E 45 58 45 29 0D 0A-24                        (.EXE)..$
-Q

What is going on. LINK always writes an .EXE. For HELLOC that file is 805 bytes: a 512-byte header, the 256 bytes that ORG 100h skipped, and the 37 bytes of program; EXE2BIN keeps only the last 37. The warning about the missing stack segment is expected for a .COM program, which uses the top of its 64 KB segment. In DEBUG, BX:CX holds the length of the file, minus 512 for an .EXE, so that W could write it back (DEBCOM2.ASM lines 792-808): 25h = 37 bytes for the .COM file and 39h = 57 bytes for the 569-byte .EXE. The .COM program's SP = FFFE points at a zero word, and offset 0 of its segment holds INT 20: a near RET from the main program would land there and end it. The .EXE program's code, data and stack are two paragraphs (20h bytes) apart, exactly as section 4.7 computed, and MOV DX,0000 is right because MSG is at offset 0 of DATA, which is now DS. Code (17 bytes, padded to 32), text (25 bytes) and stack (256 bytes) need 320 bytes, but the file holds only 57: the stack contains only DUP (?), so LINK does not store it and EXEC just reserves the room.

Questions.

  1. In the file HELLOE.EXE, which bytes hold the first instruction, and where does the header record that two of them must be changed at load time? (Use the tools of Module 5, or DEBUG's D on a renamed copy.)
  2. Change HELLOE.ASM so that ES also points at DATA. Which instruction did you add, and why is there no MOV ES,DATA?
  3. HELLOC starts with SP = FFFE although the program is 37 bytes long. Read how EXEC sets SP for a .COM file (Module 5, Listing 5.6). What would SP be if only 32 KB were free for the program and its PSP?

Lab 4.4: NASM, standard output and exit codes#

Goal. Write the same kind of program in NASM syntax, write to a handle instead of using function 09h, return an exit code, and see which output a redirection captures.

What you need. labs/04-asm/hello9.asm, hello4.asm (Example 4.2), nasm on the host, Module 6's tools/screen.asm (SCREEN.COM copies the text screen to the output of dos_run.py).

Steps.

  1. Read hello9.asm, the DEBUG program of Lab 4.2 in NASM syntax:

    Example 4.7 – labs/04-asm/hello9.asm
    ; hello9.asm - Lab 4.4: the DEBUG program again, written for NASM
; nasm -f bin -o HELLO9.COM hello9.asm
        cpu     8086
        org     100h

        mov     ah, 9                   ; print a '$'-terminated string
        mov     dx, msg
        int     21h
        mov     ax, 4C00h               ; exit with code 0
        int     21h

msg     db      'Hello from NASM', 13, 10, '$'

  2. Assemble the three programs on the host:

    Terminal
    $ nasm -f bin -o work/04/HELLO9.COM work/04/hello9.asm
$ nasm -f bin -o work/04/HELLO4.COM work/04/hello4.asm
$ nasm -f bin -o work/04/SCREEN.COM tools/screen.asm

    HELLO9.COM is 30 bytes, and its first 12 bytes are exactly those of HELLO.COM from Lab 4.2: NASM computed the 10C that you counted by hand. HELLO4.COM is 81 bytes.

  3. Run them, test the exit code with IF ERRORLEVEL, redirect both, and finally copy the screen:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 60 --file A:\HELLO9.COM=work/04/HELLO9.COM --file A:\HELLO4.COM=work/04/HELLO4.COM --file A:\SCREEN.COM=work/04/SCREEN.COM "CLS >CON" "HELLO9" "HELLO9 >OUT9.TXT" "HELLO4" "IF ERRORLEVEL 3 ECHO exit code 3 or higher" "IF ERRORLEVEL 4 ECHO exit code 4 or higher" "HELLO4 >OUT4.TXT" "DIR OUT?.TXT" "TYPE OUT4.TXT" "SCREEN"

What you should see.

Output 4.17 – Lab 4.4: handles 1 and 2, and an exit code (MS-DOS 4.00)
---- CLS  (to) CON
---- HELLO9
Hello from NASM
---- HELLO9  (to) OUT9.TXT
---- HELLO4
Price: $5, on handle 1
---- IF ERRORLEVEL 3 ECHO exit code 3 or higher
exit code 3 or higher
---- IF ERRORLEVEL 4 ECHO exit code 4 or higher
---- HELLO4  (to) OUT4.TXT
---- DIR OUT?.TXT

 Volume in drive A is DOS400LAB
 Volume Serial Number is 1988-0400
 Directory of  A:\

OUT9     TXT        17 11-09-26  11:20a
OUT4     TXT        24 11-09-26  11:20a
        2 File(s)     273920 bytes free
---- TYPE OUT4.TXT
Price: $5, on handle 1
---- SCREEN
A note on handle 2
A note on handle 2

What is going on. dos_run.py sends the standard output of each command to its own log (Module 6), so only what a program writes elsewhere stays on the screen. Function 40h takes a byte count, so hello4 can print a $, which function 09h cannot. Both > redirections caught handle 1 only: OUT9.TXT has 15 + 2 bytes and OUT4.TXT 22 + 2. The line written to handle 2 appears twice on the screen, once from each run of HELLO4, because COMMAND.COM in MS-DOS 4.00 has no syntax to redirect handle 2. The exit code 3 passed in AL to function 4Ch is what IF ERRORLEVEL tests; IF ERRORLEVEL n is true when the code is n or higher, which is why the second test printed nothing. On FreeBSD (Lab 4.6) the same three ideas appear as file descriptors 1 and 2, 2> in the shell, and $?.

Questions.

  1. hello4 ends with the DOS error code when the first write fails. Which error would a write to a closed handle return, and how could you make that happen from inside the program to test the jc fail path?
  2. Write the shortest IF ERRORLEVEL sequence that prints the exact exit code of a program that returns 0, 1, 2 or 3.
  3. HELLO9.COM and HELLO.COM share their first 12 bytes but not their length. Where do they differ, and why does that not change the code?

Lab 4.5: Single-stepping a loop and watching the flags#

Goal. Watch the arithmetic flags change, instruction by instruction, and see which instructions leave them alone.

What you need. labs/04-asm/FLAGS.SCR, tools/dos_run.py, the flag table of section 4.2.

MOV CX,3

INT 20

U 100 L 12
T 2
T 3
T 3
T 3
T 3
Q

DS=1741  ES=1741  SS=1741  CS=1741  IP=0110   OV UP EI NG NZ AC PO NC
1741:0110 CD20          INT     20
-Q

What is going on. Each R display shows the flags after the instruction just executed and the instruction about to run. FE + 1 = FF: negative (NG), eight one bits (PE), no carry. FF + 1 = 00 in eight bits: zero (ZR), a carry out of bit 7 (CY) and out of bit 3 (AC). The following DEC CX clears ZR and AC but leaves CY set: INC and DEC never touch the carry flag, so that a loop counter can run between the steps of a multi-word addition. When CX reaches 0, ZR is set and JNZ (75 FB, -5 from 010A) falls through. 1 - 4 = FD needs a borrow, which is CY again. MOV changes no flags at all: after MOV AL,7F the flags still describe the subtraction. Finally 7F + 1 = 80 is no unsigned carry (NC), but in signed terms 127 + 1 gave -128, so the overflow flag is set (OV). The processor does not know whether AL holds a signed or an unsigned number; it computes both sets of flags, and the next conditional jump chooses which to look at (JC/JA for unsigned, JO/JG for signed).

Questions.

  1. Replace ADD AL,1 by INC AL. Which flag would be different after the second pass through the loop?
  2. Read AL = FD with CY and NG set as an unsigned and as a signed result. Which conditional jump would you use after SUB AL,4 to test "AL was below 4" in each reading?
  3. Rewrite the loop with LOOP 105 instead of DEC CX and JNZ 105. How many bytes do you save, and how would the flags in Output 4.18 change?

Lab 4.6: Hello, world on FreeBSD in x86-64 assembly#

Goal. Build a program with no C library at all, look at the ELF file it becomes, and make its system call fail on purpose.

What you need. The VM with the lab files in ~/lab/04: hello.asm (Example 4.3) and hello.S.

Steps.

  1. Assemble, link and run the NASM program:

    Terminal
    $ nasm -v && nasm -f elf64 hello.asm && ld -o hello hello.o && ls -l hello.o hello && ./hello; echo "exit status $?"

  2. Build the same program written in AT&T syntax for cc, which runs the C preprocessor first, so that it can use SYS_write from <sys/syscall.h> (Listing 4.12):

    Example 4.9 – labs/04-asm/freebsd/hello.S
    /* hello.S - Lab 4.6: the same program in AT&T syntax, for cc (clang's assembler) */
/* cc -nostdlib -static -o hello-att hello.S */
#include <sys/syscall.h>

        .section .rodata
msg:    .ascii  "Hello from AT&T syntax\n"
        .set    len, . - msg

        .text
        .globl  _start
_start: movl    $SYS_write, %eax        /* source first, destination last */
        movl    $1, %edi
        leaq    msg(%rip), %rsi
        movl    $len, %edx
        syscall
        jc      fail
        movl    $SYS_exit, %eax
        xorl    %edi, %edi
        syscall
fail:   movl    %eax, %edi
        movl    $SYS_exit, %eax
        syscall
    Terminal
    $ cc -nostdlib -static -o hello-att hello.S && ./hello-att

  3. Look at the files: the ELF header, the object file with its relocations, the linked program, and the end of the AT&T version:

    Terminal
    $ file hello && readelf -h hello | grep -E "OS/ABI|Type:|Entry"
$ objdump -dr hello.o
$ objdump -d hello
$ objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn hello-att | tail -12

  4. Close standard output (>&-) and run the program again, alone and under truss:

    Terminal
    $ ./hello >&-; echo "exit status $?"
$ truss -o truss.out ./hello >&-; cat truss.out

What you should see.
