Output 4.21 – Lab 4.6, step 4: a write to a closed descriptor (captured in the course VM)
$ ./hello >&-; echo "exit status $?"
exit status 9
$ truss -o truss.out ./hello >&-; cat truss.out
write(1,"Hello from x86-64 assembly\n",27)       ERR#9 'Bad file descriptor'
_exit(0x9)
process exit, rval = 9

What is going on. The whole program is 1,192 bytes: no start-up code, no C library, just _start and three system calls. In the object file the lea has a displacement of 0 and a relocation: "put here the distance to .rodata, minus 4". The minus 4 is there because a RIP-relative displacement counts from the end of the instruction, and the 4-byte field ends 4 bytes after it starts (at 0x11). ld placed .rodata at 0x200120 and the instruction's end at 0x201151, so it wrote 0x200120 - 0x201151 = -0x1031, the bytes cf ef ff ff. The source says jc and the disassembler says jb: they are two names for the same opcode, 72 (in unsigned comparisons, "carry" means "below"). The AT&T version disassembles to the same instructions, at other addresses and with a shorter message (0x17 bytes); in its source the operands are the other way round, with $ before constants and % before registers. With descriptor 1 closed, the kernel returns EBADF (9) in RAX with the carry flag set; the program passes it to exit, and truss shows the failed write exactly as in section 4.6.

Questions.

  1. The kernel takes the system call number from the saved RAX, but the program only sets EAX. Why is that enough? Assemble mov rax, 4 with NASM and look at the bytes: what did NASM do, and why is it allowed to?
  2. Compute the displacement in the leaq of hello-att from the two addresses in Output 4.20, and check it against the instruction.
  3. Which line of hello.asm would you change so that a failed write ends the program with exit status 1 instead of the error number? Why might a shell script prefer one or the other?

Lab 4.7: A real system call stub from libsys#

Goal. Read, instruction by instruction, the code that every C program on FreeBSD 15.1 runs to make the write system call, and watch the registers on both sides of the syscall instruction.

What you need. The VM, callwrite.c and wstep.gdb in ~/lab/04. Module 2 (Listings 2.9 and 2.10) shows the SYS.h macros that generate the stub and the cerror code it jumps to on failure; Module 5 explains shared libraries and the dynamic linker.

Steps.

  1. Disassemble the stub in libsys, the library that holds the system call stubs in FreeBSD 15, and see which names point to it in libsys and in libc:

    Terminal
    $ objdump -d --disassemble-symbols=__sys_write /lib/libsys.so.7
$ nm -D --defined-only /lib/libsys.so.7 | grep -w -e write -e _write -e __sys_write
$ nm -D --defined-only /lib/libc.so.7 | grep -w -e write -e _write -e __sys_write

  2. Disassemble write itself, the function a C program calls:

    Terminal
    $ objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn --disassemble-symbols=write /lib/libc.so.7

  3. Build and run a small program that calls write twice, once successfully and once on a descriptor that is not open:

    Example 4.10 – labs/04-asm/freebsd/callwrite.c
    /* callwrite.c - Lab 4.7: two write(2) calls to follow in gdb */
#include <errno.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int
main(void)
{
	ssize_t n;

	n = write(1, "hi\n", 3);
	printf("write(1) returned %zd\n", n);
	n = write(99, "hi\n", 3);
	printf("write(99) returned %zd, errno %d\n", n, errno);
	return (0);
}
    Terminal
    $ cc -g -O0 -o callwrite callwrite.c && ./callwrite && ldd callwrite

  4. Follow both calls with gdb. The script stops at the stub, steps to the syscall instruction, prints the registers, lets the kernel run, and prints them again; for the second call it also steps into cerror:

    Example 4.11 – labs/04-asm/freebsd/wstep.gdb
    # wstep.gdb - Lab 4.7: follow write(2) through the libsys stub
# gdb -batch -x wstep.gdb ./callwrite
set pagination off
set breakpoint pending on
break __sys_write
run

x/5i $pc
stepi 2
info registers rax rdi rsi rdx r10 rcx r11 rip
tbreak *($pc + 2)
continue
info registers rax rdx rcx r8 r9 r10 r11 eflags rip
continue
tbreak *($pc + 10)
continue
info registers rax rdx rcx r8 r9 r10 r11 eflags rip
stepi
x/3i $pc
finish
continue

    $ gdb -batch -x wstep.gdb ./callwrite 2>&1

What is going on. The stub is five instructions and 17 bytes:

Address Bytes Instruction Why
1b4a0 b8 04 00 00 00 mov $4,%eax system call number SYS_write (Listing 4.12); writing EAX clears the top of RAX
1b4a5 49 89 ca mov %rcx,%r10 syscall overwrites RCX, so the fourth argument travels in R10
1b4a8 0f 05 syscall enter the kernel (section 4.5)
1b4aa 0f 82 58 c9 ff ff jb (= jc) carry set: the call failed, go to cerror
1b4b0 c3 ret success: RAX already holds the result

The arguments are not touched: the C caller already put them in RDI, RSI and RDX, the same registers the kernel reads. libsys exports the stub as __sys_write and, weakly, as _write, which is why gdb calls it _write. In the shared libc the same two names are only placeholders of size 0: its build empties the stub bodies (Makefile.inc lines 8-9; only the static libc.a keeps working stubs). Its write is a different, longer function, one line of C (write.c lines 37-42): it asks __libc_interposing_slot for slot 0x1f, INTERPOS_write, of a table of function pointers, and jumps through it (libc_private.h lines 260-262). Another library, such as the threads library, can replace the pointer with its own version of write; without it the pointer leads to __sys_write in libsys. Because write ends with a jump, not a call, the backtrace goes straight from the stub to main.

The registers tell the rest. Before syscall: RAX = 4, RDI = 1, RSI the address of "hi\n", RDX = 3, and R10 equal to RCX. After the successful call: RAX = 3 (bytes written), carry clear (eflags 0x206), RCX holds the address of the instruction after syscall and R11 holds the flags (the processor put them there to return), and the kernel zeroed R8, R9 and R10 so as not to leak kernel values (Study case 4.B). After the failed call: RAX = 9, which is EBADF, and the carry flag set (eflags 0x207); jb goes to cerror (objdump names the target after the nearest exported symbol, vfork+0x18, gdb has the full symbol table and says .cerror), which stores the 9 in errno and returns -1. The third stop is a write that callwrite.c does not contain: printf buffered its two lines (standard output is a pipe here, not a terminal) and the C library flushes them with write when main returns. The script ends there, so those two lines never appear.

Run the script a few times and you may get a different picture after the first syscall. In this run, captured with an earlier version of the script, RCX, R8 and R10 came back with their old values:

Output 4.25 – The same stop in another run: the kernel returned by the other path (captured in the course VM)
Temporary breakpoint 2, _write () at _write.S:4
4       in _write.S
rax            0x3                 3
rdx            0x3                 3
rcx            0x80057c7d0         34365491152
r8             0x2016b0            2102960
r9             0x0                 0
r10            0x80057c7d0         34365491152
r11            0x206               518
eflags         0x206               [ PF IF ]
rip            0x80057a4aa         0x80057a4aa <_write+10>

Both are correct. The kernel has two ways back to user mode, sysretq and iretq, and it chose the second in that run; Study case 4.B shows the code and the reason.

Questions.

  1. Why does the stub copy RCX to R10 but leave RDI, RSI and RDX alone? Which libsys stubs would need no mov %rcx,%r10 at all? (Look at the number of arguments.)
  2. After the successful call, list every register that changed besides RAX, and say who changed it: the processor or the kernel.
  3. The jb is encoded with 6 bytes (0f 82 and a 32-bit distance), the one in hello (Lab 4.6) with 2. Why could the linker not use the short form here?

Lab 4.8: One function, two machines#

Goal. Write the same function, the sum of an array, for the 8086 under MS-DOS and for x86-64 under FreeBSD, call it, and look at its stack frame on both.

What you need. labs/04-asm/sum16.asm and SUM.SCR; in the VM sum64.asm, sumtest.c, csum.c and sum.gdb. The calling conventions are those of section 4.5 (Figure 4.4).

Steps.

  1. Read sum16.asm. main pushes the two arguments right to left, calls sum, and removes them; sum builds a frame with BP, saves SI, and returns the result in AX:

    Example 4.12 – labs/04-asm/sum16.asm (the function and its call; printdec is left out)
    main:   mov     ax, count
        push    ax                      ; second argument: n
        mov     ax, table
        push    ax                      ; first argument: the address
        call    sum                     ; AX = sum
        add     sp, 4                   ; the caller removes the arguments
        call    printdec                ; print AX in decimal
        mov     ax, 4C00h               ; exit with code 0
        int     21h

; int sum(int *a, int n): arguments on the stack, result in AX
sum:    push    bp                      ; save the caller's BP
        mov     bp, sp                  ; [bp+2] = return address
        push    si                      ; SI belongs to the caller
        mov     si, [bp+4]              ; a
        mov     cx, [bp+6]              ; n
        xor     ax, ax                  ; sum = 0
        jcxz    .done                   ; n = 0: nothing to add
.next:  add     ax, [si]
        add     si, 2                   ; next word
        loop    .next                   ; CX = CX - 1, repeat while CX != 0
.done:  pop     si
        pop     bp
        ret

  2. Assemble it on the host, run it, and run it again under DEBUG with a breakpoint after the frame is built (G 11A) and one at the RET (G 12D); SUM.SCR also dumps the 12 bytes at the top of the stack:

    Terminal
    $ nasm -f bin -o work/04/SUM16.COM work/04/sum16.asm
$ python tools/dos_run.py --timeout 60 --file A:\SUM16.COM=work/04/SUM16.COM --file A:\SUM.SCR=work/04/SUM.SCR "SUM16" "DEBUG SUM16.COM <SUM.SCR"

  3. In the VM, read sum64.asm, the same function for the System V ABI, and sumtest.c, which calls it from C:

    Example 4.13 – labs/04-asm/freebsd/sum64.asm
    ; sum64.asm - Lab 4.8: the same function for x86-64 (System V ABI), NASM syntax
; nasm -f elf64 sum64.asm
        section .text
        global  sum
; long sum(const long *a, long n): a in RDI, n in RSI, result in RAX
sum:    push    rbp                     ; a frame like the 8086 version
        mov     rbp, rsp                ; (a leaf function does not need it)
        xor     eax, eax                ; sum = 0 (writing EAX clears all of RAX)
        test    rsi, rsi
        jz      .done                   ; n = 0: nothing to add
.next:  add     rax, [rdi]
        add     rdi, 8                  ; next long
        dec     rsi
        jnz     .next
.done:  pop     rbp
        ret

        section .note.GNU-stack noalloc noexec nowrite progbits
    Example 4.14 – labs/04-asm/freebsd/sumtest.c
    /* sumtest.c - Lab 4.8: call the assembly function sum() from C */
#include <stdio.h>

long sum(const long *a, long n);

static const long table[] = { 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 6000, 7000,
    8000, 9000, 10000 };

int
main(void)
{
	printf("%ld\n", sum(table, sizeof(table) / sizeof(table[0])));
	return (0);
}

  4. Build, run, disassemble, and stop in sum after its frame is built (sum.gdb sets a breakpoint at sum+4, prints the argument registers and the top of the stack, then finishes). Finally compare with the code the compiler writes for the same loop in C (csum.c):

    Terminal

$ objdump -d sum64.o
$ gdb -batch -x sum.gdb ./sumtest 2>&1
$ cc -O1 -S -o - csum.c | sed -n "/^csum:/,/cfi_endproc/p" | grep -v cfi
$ cc -O2 -S -o - csum.c | sed -n "/^csum:/,/cfi_endproc/p" | grep -c "^[[:space:]][a-z]"
$ cc -O2 -S -o - csum.c | sed -n "/^csum:/,/cfi_endproc/p" | grep -E "paddq|movdqu" | head -4

        movdqu  16(%rdi,%rax,8), %xmm2

What is going on. At G 11A the 8086 stack holds, from SP = FFF4 upwards: the saved SI (0000), the saved BP (0000, where BP now points), the return address 010B (the add sp,4 after the call), the first argument 0154 (the address of table), the second argument 000A, and at FFFE the zero word that EXEC put there for every .COM program. DEBUG even computes [BP+04] for you: SS:FFFA=0154. At the RET, AX = D6D8, which is 55000. On x86-64 nothing is on the stack but the return address (0x201673, main+35) and the saved RBP: the two arguments arrived in RDI (the address of table) and RSI (10), and the result leaves in RAX. sum64 saves no other register because RDI, RSI and RAX are scratch registers in the System V convention, whereas SI must survive a call in the MS-DOS C convention. NASM's local labels .next and .done became the symbols sum.next and sum.done in the object file. The compiler's -O1 loop has the same four instructions plus a compare (it counts n + 1 down to 1, a consequence of n-- > 0 on a signed number), and its -O2 version, 44 instructions long, adds two longs at a time in the 128-bit XMM registers (movdqu, paddq): hand-written assembly is not automatically faster.

Questions.

  1. Draw the 8086 stack at G 11A and the x86-64 stack at sum+4 side by side, with addresses. Which entries exist on only one of them?
  2. sum16 would add up to 32,767 correctly only as signed numbers; 55000 printed correctly anyway. Why? What would sum16 print for ten copies of 10000?
  3. Remove push rbp, mov rbp, rsp and pop rbp from sum64.asm. Does sumtest still work? Which tools (debuggers, profilers) lose something, and what?

Study cases#

Study case 4.A: $GET_VERSION, instruction by instruction#

The simplest MS-DOS function is "get version": MOV AH,30h, INT 21h, and the version comes back in AX. Following it instruction by instruction shows how an MS-DOS function reads its arguments and how it returns results, which is not by setting registers.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.15 – The whole of function 30h (GETSET.ASM lines 80-114)Source ↗
BREAK <$Get_Version -- Return DOS version number>
        procedure   $GET_VERSION,NEAR
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING,ES:NOTHING

; Inputs:
;       None
; Function:
;       Return DOS version number
; Outputs:
;       OEM number in BH
;       User number in BL:CX (24 bits)
;       Version number as AL.AH in binary
;       NOTE: On pre 1.28 DOSs AL will be zero

        context DS
        MOV     BX,[USERNUM + 2]
        MOV     CX,[USERNUM]
        MOV     AX,[MSVERS]
        invoke  get_user_stack
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        MOV     [SI.user_BX],BX
        MOV     [SI.user_CX],CX
        CMP     CS:[Fake_Count],0FFH               ;AN008;
        JZ      reg                                ;AN008;
        CMP     CS:[Fake_Count],0                  ;AN008;
        JZ      usual                              ;AN008;
        DEC     CS:[Fake_Count]                    ;AN008;
reg:                                               ;AN008;
        CMP     CS:[Special_version],0             ;AN006;
        JZ      usual                              ;AN006;
        MOV     AX,CS:[Special_version]            ;AN006;
usual:                                             ;AN006;
        MOV     [SI.user_AX],AX         ; Really only sets AH
        return
EndProc $GET_VERSION

We enter the program of Output 4.9 again and let DEBUG run it into MS-DOS. INTSTEP.SCR traces the INT 21 (Outputs 4.8 and 4.9), then sets a breakpoint at $GET_VERSION with G 2C1:1D6F, unassembles it and traces two more instructions. INTOVER.SCR executes the same INT 21 with P instead, which runs the whole call and stops after it, then dumps the variables that the function read:

The address 1D6F and the names below come from MSDOS.MAP, the map file that LINK wrote when we built MS-DOS; DEBUG knows no names. Read with the listing at hand, the call goes like this:

Step Instruction(s) Effect
1 INT 21 pushes flags, CS and IP on the caller's stack; CS:IP = 02C1:1716, COMMAND in the map (Output 4.9)
2 dispatcher (Module 2, Listings 2.2 to 2.4) pushes the caller's registers on the caller's stack in the order of user_environ, stores that SS:SP in user_SP (0584 in the map), switches to SS = 02C1, SP = DskStack (0920), and calls the function through the table
3 context DS = PUSH SS, POP DS DS = DOSGROUP; at the breakpoint SP = 091E, one return address below DskStack
4 MOV BX,[03B4], MOV CX,[03B2], MOV AX,[0D12] USERNUM + 2, USERNUM, MSVERS: FF00, 0000, 0004 (Output 4.29)
5 CALL 18D5, Get_User_Stack is CS: LDS SI,[0584], RET: DS:SI now points at the caller's saved registers
6 MOV [SI+02],BX, MOV [SI+04],CX overwrite the saved BX and CX (offsets 2 and 4 of user_environ)
7 Fake_Count, Special_version checks a version number that MS-DOS can be told to report instead of its own (MS_TABLE.ASM lines 703-704); inactive here
8 MOV [SI.user_AX],AX, RET overwrite the saved AX; the dispatcher then pops all saved registers and executes IRET

user_environ is the layout of the registers that the dispatcher pushed (DOSSYM.INC lines 58-71): user_AX at offset 0, user_BX at 2, user_CX at 4, up to the IP, CS and flags pushed by INT itself. A function returns its results by writing into the saved image, and the registers are reloaded from it. The one exception is AL: on the way out the dispatcher copies the function's AL into the saved user_AX (DISP.ASM line 412), which is why the comment in Listing 4.15 says that the store into user_AX "really only sets AH". Errors work the same way: the carry flag the caller sees is a bit that the error path sets in user_F (Module 2, section 2.2.3). FreeBSD does exactly the same with its trapframe: cpu_set_syscall_retval stores the result in tf_rax and the error flag in tf_rflags (Module 2, Listing 2.13), and the return path reloads the registers from there (Study case 4.B). Output 4.29 confirms the result: AX = 0004 (version 4.00, AL major, AH minor), BX = FF00 (OEM number FF), CX = 0000, exactly the bytes at 02C1:03B2 and 02C1:0D12.

Now look at the two T commands at the end of Output 4.28. PUSH SS stores 02C1 at SS:091C, and the very next POP DS loads 7C4D from the same place. Between the two instructions, DEBUG printed the register display, and it prints with function 40h, "write to a handle" (MSGSERV.ASM lines 1490-1495). MS-DOS was still inside our function 30h, and it is not reentrant (Module 2, section 2.2.4): the dispatcher put DEBUG's call on the same DskStack (DISP.ASM line 376, in Module 2's Listing 2.4), and that call's words overwrote ours. The dispatcher does keep one earlier user_SP aside, in NSP, as a provision for INT 24h handlers (DISP.ASM lines 273-282), so the way back to our program survives; but the function now continues with DS = 7C4D and would read USERNUM and MSVERS from the wrong segment. Tracing into MS-DOS with T changes what it traces; to see results, step over the call with P. On FreeBSD a user debugger cannot step into the kernel at all (in Lab 4.7, stepi over syscall lands on the next user instruction), and every thread that enters the kernel has its own kernel stack, so one thread's system call cannot overwrite another's.

Questions. (1) Which instruction of the dispatcher stores user_SP, and which one later reloads the caller's SS:SP? (2) Why does Get_User_Stack need a CS: prefix? (3) How would $GET_VERSION have to change to return the version in DX as well?

Study case 4.B: Anatomy of one write system call#

Lab 4.7 showed the user side of write(1, "hi\n", 3). Here is the complete path, with each step at the level of instructions:

  1. The stub (Output 4.22): mov $4,%eax, mov %rcx,%r10, syscall. The three arguments are already in RDI, RSI, RDX.
  2. The processor: syscall saves RIP in RCX and RFLAGS in R11, clears the flags named in a model-specific register (among them IF and TF), loads the kernel's CS and SS, and jumps to fast_syscall (section 4.5).
  3. Entry (Module 2, Listing 2.11): swapgs, switch to the thread's kernel stack, build a struct trapframe (Listing 4.13) on it. Note what is saved where: RCX (the return address) goes into tf_rip, R11 into tf_rflags, and R10, the fourth argument, into tf_rcx (exception.S lines 544-546). Then call amd64_syscall.
  4. C code: amd64_syscall and syscallenter look up entry 4 of the system call table, copy the arguments out of the trapframe and call sys_write (Module 2, section 2.2.5); the file system code writes the 3 bytes. cpu_set_syscall_retval stores 3 in tf_rax and clears PSL_C in tf_rflags, or on an error stores the error number and sets PSL_C (Module 2, Listing 2.13).
  5. Return, in assembly again:
FreeBSD 15.1Listing 4.16 – The two ways back to user mode (exception.S lines 571-600)Source ↗
1:      movq    PCPU(CURPCB),%rax
        /* Disable interrupts before testing PCB_FULL_IRET. */
        cli
        testl   $PCB_FULL_IRET,PCB_FLAGS(%rax)
        jnz     4f
        /* Check for and handle AST's on return to userland. */
        movq    PCPU(CURTHREAD),%rax
        cmpl    $0,TD_AST(%rax)
        jne     3f
        call    handle_ibrs_exit
        callq   *mds_handler
        /* Restore preserved registers. */
        movq    TF_RDI(%rsp),%rdi       /* bonus; preserve arg 1 */
        movq    TF_RSI(%rsp),%rsi       /* bonus: preserve arg 2 */
        movq    TF_RDX(%rsp),%rdx       /* return value 2 */
        movq    TF_RAX(%rsp),%rax       /* return value 1 */
        movq    TF_RFLAGS(%rsp),%r11    /* original %rflags */
        movq    TF_RIP(%rsp),%rcx       /* original %rip */
        movq    TF_RSP(%rsp),%rsp       /* user stack pointer */
        xorl    %r8d,%r8d               /* zero the rest of GPRs */
        xorl    %r10d,%r10d
        cmpq    $~0,PCPU(UCR3)
        je      2f
        movq    PCPU(UCR3),%r9
        andq    PCPU(UCR3_LOAD_MASK),%r9
        movq    %r9,%cr3
2:      xorl    %r9d,%r9d
        movq    $PMAP_UCR3_NOMASK,PCPU(UCR3_LOAD_MASK)
        swapgs
        sysretq

With interrupts disabled, the code checks two things. If the thread's PCB has the flag PCB_FULL_IRET, it jumps to doreti, the general return path of interrupts and traps, which reloads every register from the trapframe and ends with iretq. If an AST is pending (a signal to deliver, a reschedule), it handles it with interrupts enabled and checks again. Otherwise it takes the fast path: it reloads only RDI, RSI, RDX and RAX from the trapframe, puts the saved flags in R11 and the saved RIP in RCX for sysretq, restores the user's stack pointer, and zeroes R8, R9 and R10 rather than leave kernel values in them; the other registers are callee-saved in C, so the kernel's C code has preserved the user's values. sysretq copies RCX to RIP and R11 to RFLAGS and drops to user mode.

That is exactly what the two runs of Lab 4.7 showed:

Register after syscall sysretq path (Output 4.24) iretq path (Output 4.25) Why
RAX 3 3 tf_rax, the result
RCX 0x80057a4aa (the next instruction) 0x80057c7d0 (its old value) sysretq needs RCX; doreti restores tf_rcx, the copy of R10
R8, R10 0 old values zeroed on the fast path, restored from the trapframe on the slow one
R11 0x206 0x206 sysretq takes the flags from R11; doreti reloads R11 from the trapframe
carry flag clear clear PSL_C in tf_rflags

Both paths honour the contract of the stub, which only promises RAX and the carry flag; the C caller assumes that RCX, R8 to R11 are destroyed by any call anyway. Who sets PCB_FULL_IRET? Among others, the context switch code, every time a thread leaves the processor (cpu_switch.S lines 86-88), because the user's segment registers and bases must then be reloaded, and ptrace when a debugger changes the registers, for example its program counter (ptrace_machdep.c lines 400-407). doreti clears it again (exception.S lines 1152-1154), and so does fast_syscall itself, just before it enables interrupts (exception.S lines 549-551). So in the run of Output 4.25 the flag was set during the call itself, most likely by a context switch: the thread left the processor while the write was in progress, or in ast for a reschedule. Which path a call takes depends on timing, not on the program.

Side by side with Study case 4.A:

MS-DOS 4.00, INT 21h FreeBSD 15.1, syscall
Entry instruction INT 21h: pushes flags, CS, IP syscall: pushes nothing; RIP goes to RCX, RFLAGS to R11
Privilege change none ring 3 to ring 0
Saved registers on the caller's stack (user_environ) on the thread's kernel stack (struct trapframe)
Kernel stack one of three fixed stacks for the whole system one per thread
Result written into user_AX and friends written into tf_rax, tf_rdx
Error carry bit in user_F, code in user_AX PSL_C in tf_rflags, code in tf_rax
Return instruction IRET sysretq, or iretq through doreti
Reentrant no (Study case 4.A) yes

Questions. (1) Why must the fast path disable interrupts before testing the flags, and when are they enabled again? (2) Suppose the kernel forgot xorl %r8d,%r8d. What could a user program learn, and why does that matter? (3) The MS-DOS row "Kernel stack" says "three fixed stacks". Which are they, and which functions use which (Module 2, Listing 2.4)?

Study case 4.C: Macros as a language#

The MS-DOS kernel is written in MASM, but it does not read like plain 8086 code: almost every procedure starts with procedure, calls others with invoke, returns with return or retz, and sets segment registers with context. These are macros from DOSMAC.INC, and together they form a small language on top of the assembler. Counting the lines that begin with each macro name (labels allowed, comments excluded) in the 83 .ASM files of v4.0/src/DOS gives:

Macro Uses Expands to
invoke 799 CALL name, plus EXTRN name:NEAR in pass 2 if name is not defined in this file
procedure 395 PUBLIC name, name PROC, and a stack-depth check at the end
return 391 RET, remembering its address in ret_l
SaveReg / RestoreReg 270 one PUSH or POP per register, counting the depth
transfer 148 JMP name (through the jump macro, short when possible), plus EXTRN like invoke
retz, retnz, retc, retnc 141 a conditional jump to a nearby RET, or a jump around a new one
context 136 PUSH SS, POP reg

invoke exists because of the linker: a CALL to a procedure in another file needs an EXTRN declaration, and invoke writes it only when needed (DOSMAC.INC lines 58-67). context encodes a fact about the kernel's run time: while MS-DOS runs, SS always holds DOSGROUP (the dispatcher set it), so copying SS is the cheapest way to point another segment register at the kernel's data. The conditional returns are the most interesting:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.17 – return, condret, retz and context (DOSMAC.INC lines 265-340)Source ↗
return  macro x
    local a
.xcref
a:
        RET
ret_l = a
.cref
endm
.xcref  return
⋮
condret macro   cc,ncc
    local   a
.xcref
.xcref a
.cref
    ifdef   ret_l                       ;; if ret_l is defined
        if (($ - ret_l) le 126) and ($ gt ret_l)
                                        ;;     if ret_l is near enough then
            a:  j&cc    ret_l           ;;         a: j<CC> to ret_l
            ret_&cc = a                 ;;         define ret_<CC> to be a:
            exitm
        endif
    endif
    ifdef   ret_&cc                     ;; if ret_<CC> defined
        if (($ - ret_&cc) le 126) and ($ gt ret_&cc)
                                        ;;     if ret_<CC> is near enough
            a:  j&cc    ret_&cc         ;;         a: j<CC> to ret_<CC>
            ret_&cc = a                 ;;         define ret_<CC> to be a:
            exitm
        endif
    endif
    j&ncc   a                           ;; j<NCC> a:
    return                              ;; return
    a:                                  ;; a:
    ret_&cc = ret_l                     ;; define ret_<CC> to be ret_l
endm
.xcref  condret

BREAK <RETZ - return if zero, links up shortwise if necessary>
⋮
retz    macro
    condret z,nz
endm
.xcref  retz
⋮
context macro   r
        PUSH    SS
        POP     r
        ASSUME  r:DOSGROUP
endm
.xcref  context

The 8086 has no "return if zero" instruction, and its conditional jumps reach only 127 bytes forward or 128 back. return emits a RET and records its address in the assembler variable ret_l. retz then emits JZ ret_l if that RET is behind it and within reach: two bytes instead of three. If no RET is near, it emits the opposite jump over a new RET. And because every such jump is itself a place that "returns if zero", it records its own address as ret_z, so that the next retz can jump to the jump. This is a small optimiser written in the macro language, running at assembly time.

labs/04-asm/MACDEMO.ASM uses the macros in three tiny procedures. Copy DOSMAC.INC next to it (the include file tests a symbol DEBUG at line 376, so MACDEMO.ASM defines it) and assemble it with a listing:

Terminal
$ cp src-ext/MS-DOS/v4.0/src/INC/DOSMAC.INC work/04/
$ python tools/dos_tools.py --timeout 120 --dir work/04 "MASM MACDEMO,,MACDEMO;"
Output 4.30 – MASM messages for MACDEMO.ASM (run with tools/dos_tools.py)
---- MASM MACDEMO,,MACDEMO;
Microsoft (R) Macro Assembler Version 5.10
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corp 1981, 1988.  All rights reserved.

CountChars... pass 1
IsEmpty... pass 1
Unbalanced... pass 1
CountChars... pass 2
IsEmpty... pass 2
Unbalanced... pass 2
***** Possible stack size error in Unbalanced *****

  47616 + 414534 Bytes symbol space free

      0 Warning Errors
      0 Severe  Errors
Output 4.31 – Two expansions of retz in MACDEMO.LST
 000E  0B C9                            OR      CX,CX
                                        retz                            ; nothing to do if the string is empty
                             1      condret z,nz
                             2  .xcref
                             2  .xcref ??0000
                             2  .cref
                             2      ifdef   ret_l                       ;
                             2      endif
                             2      ifdef   ret_z                     ;
⋮
                             2      endif
 0010  75 01                 2      jnz   ??0000                           ;
                             2      return                              ;
                             3  .xcref
 0012                        3  ??0001:
 0012  C3                    3          RET
 = 0012                      3  ret_l = ??0001
                             3  .cref
 0013                        2      ??0000:                                  ;
 = 0012                      2      ret_z = ret_l                     ;
                                        context ES                      ; ES = DOSGROUP, as the kernel does
 0013  16                    1          PUSH    SS
 0014  07                    1          POP     ES
                             1          ASSUME  ES:DOSGROUP
                                        return
                             1  .xcref
 0015                        1  ??0002:
 0015  C3                    1          RET
 = 0015                      1  ret_l = ??0002
⋮
 0016                        1  IsEmpty    PROC    NEAR
 = 0000                      1          ?initstack    = ?stackdepth     ;
 0016  80 3C 24                         CMP     BYTE PTR [SI],'$'
                                        retz                            ; a short jump to an earlier RET
                             1      condret z,nz
                             2  .xcref
                             2  .xcref ??0003
                             2  .cref
                             2      ifdef   ret_l                       ;
                             2          if (($ - ret_l) le 126) and ($ gt ret_l)
                             2                                          ;
 0019  74 FA                 2              ??0003:  jz    ret_l           ;
 = 0019                      2              ret_z = ??0003                 ;
                             2              exitm
 001B  80 3C 00                         CMP     BYTE PTR [SI],0
                                        return
                             1  .xcref
 001E                        1  ??0004:
 001E  C3                    1          RET

The first retz, in CountChars, finds no RET before it, so it expands to JNZ over a new RET (75 01, C3) and records that RET as ret_z. The second, in IsEmpty, finds ret_l = 0015, the return at the end of CountChars, 4 bytes behind it, and emits JZ to it: 74 FA, a displacement of -6 counted from the end of the jump at 001B. The procedure has no RET of its own for the zero case: it borrows its neighbour's. The %OUT lines show the procedure macro announcing itself in both passes, and EndProc comparing the stack depth counted by SaveReg and RestoreReg: Unbalanced pushes BX and never pops it, and the macro catches it. The macro procedure prologue is:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 4.18 – The procedure macro (DOSMAC.INC lines 132-145)Source ↗
procedure   MACRO   name,distance
        ?frame =    0
        ?aframe =   2                   ;; remember the pushed BP
        PUBLIC  name
        IF1
        %OUT name... pass 1
        ENDIF
        IF2
        %OUT name... pass 2
        ENDIF
name    PROC    distance
        ?initstack    = ?stackdepth     ;; beginning of procedure
ENDM
.xcref  procedure

EndProc (Module 0 shows it) compares ?stackdepth with the ?initstack remembered here. NASM has the same power (%macro, %if, %assign, context-local labels); on FreeBSD the C preprocessor plays this role for assembly files written for cc, as the SYS.h macros that generate every libsys stub show (Module 2, Listing 2.9).

Questions. (1) Why is retz 2 bytes in IsEmpty but 3 in CountChars? (2) What would happen to IsEmpty if someone inserted 130 bytes of code between the two procedures? (3) Write a NASM macro context that does the same as MASM's.

Homework#

Exercise 4.1: Decoding by hand, three times#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

Tasks:

  1. Output 4.13 shows the first bytes of FreeBSD's /boot/boot0. Decode by hand the 19 bytes that follow the ones of Lab 4.1, at 7C0C to 7C1E: 89 E6 BF 00 06 B9 00 01 F3 A5 89 FD B1 08 F3 AB FE 45 F2. For each instruction give its length, and for each ModR/M byte its three fields in binary. Then say in one sentence what the sequence does, and compute the address that the last instruction changes.
  2. The 64-bit start-up code of every C program begins with these bytes (the first 21 bytes of _start in /usr/lib/crt1.o): 55 48 89 E5 48 89 F1 48 63 07 48 8D 77 08 48 8D 54 C7 10 89 C7. Decode them by hand, marking every REX prefix (which of W, R, X, B is set?) and every SIB byte. Check with objdump -d --disassemble-symbols=_start /usr/lib/crt1.o in the VM.
  3. In the VM, run objdump -d setup.o without --triple on the object file of Output 4.6. Explain every line that differs from Output 4.6, including the ones objdump cannot decode at all.

Deliverables: your decoding sheets (scanned handwriting is fine), the objdump output of task 3 and a half-page explanation.

Hints: section 4.1 has the tables you need; F3 is a prefix. For task 1, DI has a known value after the copy loop; the comments in stand/i386/boot0/boot0.S (lines 179-197) tell you what the code means, but decode first and read afterwards. For task 2, remember that mod = 01 with r/m = 100 means "SIB byte, then an 8-bit displacement". In 64-bit mode the operand size of BC is 32 bits.

Exercise 4.2: A ROT13 filter on both systems#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 4 h.

ROT13 replaces each letter by the one 13 places further on in the alphabet, wrapping around (A becomes N, n becomes a) and leaves every other byte alone; applying it twice gives the input back.

Tasks:

  1. Write rot13d.asm, a .COM program for NASM (nasm -f bin) that reads standard input with function 3Fh into a buffer, converts the buffer, and writes it to standard output with function 40h, until 3Fh returns 0 bytes. Exit with function 4Ch and exit code 0, or with the MS-DOS error code if a call fails.
  2. Write rot13.asm for FreeBSD/amd64 (nasm -f elf64, then ld, no C library) that does the same with the system calls read, write and _exit and the syscall instruction. On an error, exit with errno as the status.
  3. Test both with a file larger than your buffer, through redirection, and show that applying the filter twice gives back the original file byte for byte (FC /B on MS-DOS, cmp on FreeBSD). On FreeBSD also test it in a pipeline and with standard input closed (./rot13 <&-), and explain the exit status you get.
  4. Report the size of both executables and of the same filter written in C and linked statically (cc -O2 -static) in the VM.

Deliverables: both sources, the transcripts of task 3, the sizes of task 4, and a short note on how each version detects end of file and errors.

Hints: read may return fewer bytes than you asked for (a pipe usually does); convert and write exactly the number of bytes it returned. A .COM program can use the memory after its last byte as the buffer, because MS-DOS gives it the whole segment. syscall destroys RCX and R11, so do not keep a count there across a call. The trick AND AL,0DFh folds lower case onto upper case for the test, but you must convert the original byte. Do not write an upcase filter: Module 5's Exercise 5.3 already has one.

Exercise 4.3: Patch a copy of a program#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

Tasks:

  1. On MS-DOS, copy HELLO4.COM (Lab 4.4) to PATCHED.COM. Without reassembling, change two bytes of the copy with a DEBUG script (E and W) so that it exits with code 7 instead of 3 and prints Price: $9 instead of Price: $5. Find the two offsets yourself from the source and Lab 4.4, run the patched copy from a batch file that tests ERRORLEVEL, and compare the files with FC /B.
  2. In the VM, copy hello (Lab 4.6) to hello.patched and change it with dd conv=notrunc so that it prints only Jello, without a newline: one byte of the message and one byte of an immediate operand. Compute the file offsets from the virtual addresses with nm, objdump -d and readelf -l, in a shell script, not by hand. Compare the two files with cmp -l.
  3. Explain why the MS-DOS patch needs no address arithmetic beyond subtracting 100h, while the FreeBSD one needs the program headers.

Deliverables: your DEBUG script and batch file, your shell script, both transcripts and the explanation.

Hints: DEBUG loads a .COM file at offset 100h and W writes back BX:CX bytes, which it sets to the file size when loading (Lab 4.3). For an ELF file, a PT_LOAD header maps filesz bytes from file offset offset to address vaddr, so offset_in_file = address - vaddr + offset.

Exercise 4.4: Counting bits, by hand and by compiler#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 4 h.

Tasks:

  1. Write popcount (the number of 1 bits in a word) in 8086 assembly for NASM, as a near procedure with the MS C calling convention (argument on the stack, result in AX), and a .COM test program that prints the result for a table of test values, including 0, 1, 8000h, FFFFh and 1234h.
  2. Write popcount64 for FreeBSD in NASM (System V convention: argument in RDI, result in EAX) and a C test program that compares it with __builtin_popcountl on at least 8 values, including ~0UL.
  3. Write the same function in C with the obvious loop (n += x & 1; x >>= 1;), and a second version with Kernighan's loop (x &= x - 1; n++;). Compile them with MS C 5.10 (CL /c /Ox /Fc) and with cc -O2 -S in the VM.
  4. Count the instructions in the loop body of each version, yours and the compilers', and make a table. Explain any instruction a compiler used that you did not, and anything a compiler did that looks wasteful.

Deliverables: the sources, the test outputs, the listings of task 3 and the table with explanations.

Hints: on the 8086, SHR reg,1 puts the bit shifted out into CF, and ADC AX,0 adds it. Use [BP+4] for the argument after PUSH BP; MOV BP,SP (section 4.5). The POPCNT instruction exists on the VM's processor, but cc uses it only when told the processor has it (-mpopcnt); look at what it does without that option.

Exercise 4.5: System calls without a library#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 4 h.

Tasks:

  1. On MS-DOS, write RAWCALL.C for MS C 5.10 that uses intdos() from <dos.h> to call function 30h and function 40h, once on handle 1 and once on handle 99, and prints AX and the carry flag after each call.
  2. In the VM, write rawcall.c with a function raw_syscall3(number, a1, a2, a3, &carry) that executes the syscall instruction through GCC-style inline assembly, and use it to call getpid, write on fd 1 and write on fd 99. Print RAX and the carry flag, and compare with what syscall(2) returns and leaves in errno for the same bad call.
  3. Write a shell script that, for read, write, close, getpid and openat, extracts the number loaded into EAX by the __sys_ stub in /lib/libsys.so.7 (as in Lab 4.7) and compares it with the SYS_ constant in <sys/syscall.h>.

Deliverables: the two programs, the script and their outputs, and a paragraph on how the two systems report an error to the caller, at the instruction level and at the C level.

Hints: in inline assembly every register that the instruction or the kernel may change must be an output or in the clobber list: Study case 4.B tells you which ones. Use the "+a", "+D", "+S" and "+d" constraints for RAX, RDI, RSI and RDX, and setc to get the carry flag into a byte. intdos returns the flags in out.x.cflag.

Exercise 4.6: Essay: what does a segment cost?#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write 1,200 to 1,500 words on the question: what does the 16-bit segmented model of the 8086 cost a programmer, compared with the flat 64-bit model of x86-64 under FreeBSD? Use at least four concrete examples from this module and from Modules 2 and 5, with references: for example context and CS: prefixes in the MS-DOS kernel (Study cases 4.A and 4.C), the 64 KB limit of a .COM file, near and far calls, the EXE relocation table (Lab 4.3), ASSUME, and on the other side RIP-relative addressing, position-independent code and the cost of a 4- or 5-level page table walk. Say also what segmentation gave MS-DOS that a flat model would not have given it on an 8086.

Deliverables: the essay, with a reference list.

Hints: separate the costs that the 8086 imposed (16-bit registers, 1 MB) from those that segmentation itself imposed (two-part addresses, overlapping segments, ASSUME). Module 5's discussion of memory models is the best place to start.

Further reading#

  • Intel Corporation, Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, volume 2 (instruction set reference, including the opcode maps and the ModR/M and SIB tables of appendix A and chapter 2) and volume 3 (SYSCALL, SYSRET, interrupts and exceptions).
  • Intel Corporation, iAPX 86/88, 186/188 User's Manual: the 8086 as the authors of MS-DOS knew it.
  • System V Application Binary Interface, AMD64 Architecture Processor Supplement (the x86-64 psABI): the calling convention of section 4.5, the stack alignment rule and the red zone.
  • The NASM manual, https://www.nasm.us/doc/: chapters on the bin and elf64 output formats, local labels and the macro language.
  • Microsoft Corporation, Microsoft Macro Assembler 5.1 Programmer's Guide: ASSUME, segments, groups and the macro language used by DOSMAC.INC.
  • Ray Duncan, Advanced MS-DOS Programming, 2nd edition, Microsoft Press, 1988: INT 21h from assembly, .COM and .EXE programs, and DEBUG.
  • FreeBSD manual pages syscall(2), intro(2), write(2), _exit(2), ptrace(2), truss(1), elf(5) and arch(7), https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=syscall&sektion=2&manpath=FreeBSD+15.1-RELEASE and neighbours, and the GDB manual, chapters "Machine Code" and "Registers".
  • The sources read in this module: v4.0/src/CMD/DEBUG, v4.0/src/INC/DOSMAC.INC, v4.0/src/DOS/GETSET.ASM, sys/amd64/amd64/exception.S, sys/x86/include/frame.h and stand/i386/boot0/boot0.S.
